subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BY PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
speechtext:
Subsection 6 of section 236 of the criminal code has to do with the exceptions in favour of lotteries. One of these exceptions is found in paragraph (e), as follows:
(e) the Art Union of London, Great Britain, or the Art Union of Ireland.
This exception is now obsolete. However, all hon. members know that quite a few sweepstakes are now being held throughout Canada. subtopic: RULE RESPECTING QUESTIONS PERMISSIBLE ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps hon. members would allow me, not with a view

to curtailing discussion in any way, but rather to enable the house to get on with its business, to draw attention to the rules with respect to asking questions on the orders of the day.
The rules do provide for an opportunity to ask questions on the orders of the day with reference to an emergent situation on which it is desirable to have immediate information from the ministry. But if hon. members will look at standing order 17, and citation 197, they will see that the rule is that:
A question which could be inserted on the order paper is not allowed on the orders of the day being called.
Yesterday we had a regular battery of questions on the orders of the day. I think most of them might have been placed on the order paper. Probably they would not have been allowed except that his honour the Speaker did not wish to prevent anyone from having as much latitude as possible. The rule which I have quoted is there for the convenience of all members of the house, and no doubt his honour the Speaker will wish to see that it is enforced as we proceed.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: RULE RESPECTING QUESTIONS PERMISSIBLE ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: Just one word in connection with what my right hon. friend has said. I quite agree that the rule is there. At the same time I think that both he and I have been impressed with the fact that in the British House of Commons the question hour is literally an hour or more; and I am wondering if it would not be to the advantage of all of us, of the house, and of the country, if in this, as in so many other things, we were to follow the British custom and permit a little more latitude in regard to questions, so that the country would have a reasonably prompt reply in regard to many matters. I am not saying this with any thought of embarrassing the government or of criticizing the remarks of the right hon. gentleman. It is merely that I believe that for the sake of good government it would be a good thing, whatever party is in power, to permit a considerable amount of latitude in regard to such matters as this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

First, in regard to what my hon. friend had to say as to the custom in the British house in answering questions on the orders of the day, the British house, like this house, is governed by its standing rules, and the rules of the British house are somewhat different from the rules here. If the rules of this house are to be changed they ought to be considered in the first instance by the appropriate committee of the house and approved by the house. So long as the

Radio-Address oj Prime Minister
rules are what they are, I think my hon. friend will agree with me that they ought to be observed.
I have not in mind at the moment the practice of the British house, but my recollection is that except questions which are of an urgent character the only kind of question which is permitted to be asked which does not appear on the orders of the day is a supplementary question arising out of a question that is already on the orders of the day; a minister may be asked-and I think it has been permitted here-if the reply is not regarded as adequate, to supplement his remarks so as to make them quite clear.
My colleague the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has drawn my attention to the wording of the rules of the British house with respect to questions. I quote the following:
No questions shall be taken after a quarter before four of the clock, except questions which have not been answered in consequence of the absence of the minister to whom they are addressed, and questions which have not appeared on the paper, but which are of an urgent character, and relate either to matters of public importance or to the arrangement of business.
The questions that are taken before that are the questions which are on the order paper.

I have a question to direct to the Prime Minister. Probably it is one of those which he thinks might have been put on the order paper, but if he takes that view I do not agree; I think it is urgent enough to require an answer to-day. I have to preface it by a remark or two. In my speech the other day in the house I offered in a general way some criticism of the right hon. gentleman about his not having travelled across the country. The right hon. gentleman replied. But last evening he made a

Radio-Address of Prime Minister
speech over the radio which, according to the press reports-I did not have the pleasure of listening to it-was a very good speech, as his speeches always are, and he made a pretty elaborate reply. I believe, to my criticism in the house. I should like to know from him, or from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) if he prefers, whether the Liberal party paid for that political broadcast over the radio last night or whether the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation presented that time as a gift to the Liberal party.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADDRESS OF PRIME MINISTER BROADCAST ON MONDAY, JANUARY 23
speechtext:
In regard to what my hon. friend has just said about my address last night, I was asked, as he was asked, by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to give one of a series of addresses relating to the business of government. I was asked to explain the position and responsibilities and duties of the prime minister and the secretary of state for external affairs and the president of the privy council in relation to the business of government. My hon. friend was asked to give an address on the duties of the leader of the opposition, who has a recognized position of responsibility in the affairs of government and is a salaried officer of parliament. My hon. friend did not take advantage of the proposal. I was asked, not by the corporation but by one of my secretaries, if I would not see him about making sure of having his address included in the series, simply to make sure that the series would be complete; but I thought that my hon. friend could decide best what he wished to do and therefore I did not say anything to him about it.
Now as to the substance of my remarks last night. As a matter of fact they were not in any way intended as a reply to any criticism on the part of my hon. friend; they were an explanation of my position as Prime Minister and as Secretary of State for External Affairs. I set forth what my duties were in that regard, some indication of the amount of time they consumed, and the extent to which, the time being consumed in the way it was, it was not possible for me as Prime Minister to do some of the things I would like to do-among others, travel about the country as frequently as I would. I may say that in my remarks I was referring to the duties not only of the present Prime Minister but of previous prime ministers and of possible future prime ministers.

subtopic: ADDRESS OF PRIME MINISTER BROADCAST ON MONDAY, JANUARY 23

cessors. I said that while all agreed that it might relieve the prime minister of some of his duties to have as the secretary of state for external affairs a member of the government holding a separate portfolio, all had found that our leading questions, our big problems in Canada, are so intimately associated with our membership in the British commonwealth of nations, or our membership in the League of Nations, or our proximity to the United States, that it was inadvisable to separate the matters of greatest concern to the Prime Minister from those of external affairs. speechtext:
I
would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we extend the question period preceding orders of the day, because it seems to me to put the house into that jocular frame of mind that makes it easy for the first speaker who rises after that period.
The speech from the throne is remarkable in two particulars: first, in its length, and second, to my mind, in the fact that it is more or less a death-bed repentance; for we

The Address-Mr. Perley
find forecast legislation that may be brought down this session which should have been brought down three or four sessions ago.
If I had time I should like to review the period in our history from 1922 down to the present time, and to discuss the records of the three governments that have been in office during that period: the King government from 1922 to 1930, the Bennett government from 1930 to 1935-the most critical period in our history, not even excepting the war period-and the regime from 1935 to the present. Time will not allow me to do this. I recall, however, that strikingly eloquent message of hope that was flashed across the dominion on the night of the election of 1935, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) promised that he would abolish poverty and adversity and bring about in Canada that condition whereby all our difficulties would be settled by peaceful and harmonious conferences with the provinces, and there would be one happy family in the dominion.
I have time only to summarize briefly what has taken place in the last-mentioned period. We find taxation the highest in Canada's history. The government still finds ways of spending more money than it receives. The annual increase in trade which they found when taking office has now become an annual decrease. Exports continue to fall. For the first ten months of last year exports to the United States declined to the extent of $140,000,000. Wheat prices are still low. The Canadian wheat board was illegally discontinued in 1936-37. Taxation has increased, the railway problem is untouched, unemployment and poverty are still with us, and no steps have been taken to strengthen interprovincial or domestic trade or to equalize the prices of primary and secondary products in the domestic market. This last feature is important and it is regrettable that no effort has been made to deal with the situation.
We have had for the last three years what has been rightly termed a do-nothing government. We have had government by commission-commissions headed by party men and party counsel, regardless of their knowledge or lack of knowledge of the subjects with which they have dealt. Lastly, in summarizing. may I point out that the social reform legislation passed by the previous government has been destroyed, partly by judicial decisions and partly by repeal, and there has been no clear hand of leadership in sight.
It is my duty to deal with one or two problems pertaining more particularly to western Canada, and I speak with special reference
to relief in Saskatchewan. In that province we have had, in connection with the distribution of relief, a system which in my opinion is a disgrace to this government and to the dominion. I am not complaining of the amount expended, because relief was necessary. Many would not have been able to carry on had it not been for relief. What I am complaining about is the manner in which relief has been distributed in the west. I am referring to the maladministration that has been and is at the present time so apparent-irregularities in the carrying out of relief, and graft in many instances. I repeat, it is a disgrace.
For example, what is going on in the northern part of the province at the present time? Many hon. members, particularly western members, are no doubt aware of what has been taking place. There, the daily press carries red headlines with reference to the evidence given in the courts where certain persons have been prosecuted. Relief has been given out promiscuously to party friends and a favoured few. Orders have been approved by inspectors, supervisors, reeves and secretaries of municipalities and others; and as one witness said before the court, "The government give, I take; thank him nicely." I have here, dated December 27, a headline that reads:
Not Sufficient Checks kept on Relief by Official.
A prominent king's counsel, when pleading for leniency for his client before the court before concurrent sentence of two and a half years was imposed on each of 332 counts for forgery and uttering relief vouchers and cheques, said there had not been sufficient check. The magistrate, in passing sentence, said the accused was only part of a crooked machine. I ask this government what system of auditing or checking is in effect in that province when a man could get away with 332 forgeries involving sums from $15 to $50.
Another headline reads: "Handed more relief than he applied for." On January 14 one witness tells of laxity in checking up municipal relief. Another headline states that direct relief was paid for in the hire of a car of one of the inspectors. The garage people were given an order for groceries. Then we are informed that the Fish Creek relief list is changed daily, and that there is laxity in the check-up. On January 17 a witness states that this check-up was not very efficient; and at the Wakaw trial it was stated that relief was granted to favourites. Again, one man swears that he got all and more than he asked for. The evidence was that it was very easy to get relief.
The Address-Mr. Perley

I have here a statement as reported in the Regina Star of January 17: " Orders for relief were handed out on election day." This is a good one. In point the witness said that some of the relief orders were distributed to people when they came to the polls. He said his father had distributed relief vouchers at his home on election day, and there was a polling booth at his home. What do hon. members think of such a condition as that being allowed to prevail in this country?
Then I have here something that I regret to have to bring to the attention of the house. It is to the effect that the party men in that province decide who shall get the jobs. This is dated January 18 and states:
No jobs for other than Liberals, says Regina M.L.A.
The reference is to the new member-elect of the provincial house and that is the statement he made to the Liberal council when he thought it was behind closed doors. The report continues:
In future, said Mr. McDaniel, "no appointment will be deemed to be properly made unless it bears the initials of Mr. Hogarth (senior member elect for Regina), Mr. McNiven (federal M.P. for Regina), or myself."
I submit that it is a sorry state of affairs when no one in that province can be considered for a position in the service, temporary or otherwise, unless he has the O.K. of these men. I do not think the hon. member for Regina (Mr. McNiven) would be a party to that; I know him too well. But he owes it to this house to make a statement repudiating this, or as to how he appears in the favoured committee that has to O.K. these positions. I think he should repudiate Mr. McDaniel's statement, and I hope he will do so. I should not like to think that he is a part of this political machine, but I have quoted that to show that there is a real machine operating in that province.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The towns named in the
information I have received I think are very near the hon. member's district. I am not sure of the towns, but I have the names of several villages and towns in which these tokens were in use. It is very prevalent in all the northern part of the province, and it is a wonder to me if the hon. member'3 district has escaped. We have inspectors, supervisors and reeves issuing orders even from the cars during the election campaign. Gas coupons are being issued and used at filling stations. There is political patronage in that province that should be cleared up.
I now ask the government to consider, even at this late date, the setting up of a national relief administration or commission to handle the distribution of relief in Saskatchewan from now on, such a commission as we had from 1930 to 1935. I demand that the government take the suggestion into consideration with a view to clearing this thing up. Such a commission should be appointed in due course. The condition I have outlined has perhaps not been prevalent in every part of the province; in the central part I

The Address-Mr. Perley
do not think it has prevailed. I know many of the municipal clerks and reeves and councillors in my district; many of these councils are composed of men who have a sense of responsibility and duty, and I am sure it would not be safe to suggest anything such as this to them.
I regret to have to inform the house that owing to a blunder or incompetence on the part of someone last spring, seed was not delivered to the farmers in proper time in the areas in which it was required. Distribution of seed wheat was late. In some cases one farmer had his seed and got it in in proper time, while his neighbour had not, and there was a difference of five to ten bushels an acre in the crops. That condition should be inquired into with a view to finding out who was responsible. We know that the municipalities had prepared their statements and estimates, had arranged their credits at the bank; we know that the board had the order from the government to convert the options into seed, and we know that there was blundering somewhere, and the people in that western country through the lateness of distribution of seed suffered a loss of at least S30.000,000. We know what that means to eastern Canada and to labour and transportation. The loss is so serious that it is the concern of this dominion to know who blundered, because we do not want it to recur this spring.
If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) were in his seat I should like to ask him to state when this matter of seed wheat is going to be dealt with in this house. When does he propose to bring down his bill providing for seed? Last year he will recall that he asked some of us on this side to refrain from asking questions. In order to facilitate the passing of the bill we did so, but we want to know this year that the bill will come down in time to permit of proper distribution of seed for spring seeding. I have here a resolution which has come to hand in to-day's press. If hon. members care to look it up in the reading room they will see that the association of rural municipalities have protested the delay in the seed distribution in 1938 and requested the government to take action in proper time this year.
I should like to deal with the live stock industry as it affects us in the west. As far as Saskatchewan is concerned it has been struck a blow from which it will not recover for many years. I regret that the Minister of Agriculture was not more concerned last year when there was a demand from farmers in many western rural districts for an increase in
the number of sires. I hope that this year he will give proper consideration to the matter and see that it is dealt with efficiently. The live stock industry is in a precarious position, and I urge upon the minister that he take every possible step to foster that industry and restore it to the position it held a few years ago.
The marketing question is also important. I am pleased to note that in the speech from the throne it is indicated that the government may take some action to improve the marketing of our primary products. I have prepared a resolution on this subject and have it ready for the order paper, but unfortunately the procedure does not permit me to have two resolutions on the order paper at the same time. But I ask the government to take some action looking to the passing of the necessary legislation. It may be providing for marketing boards to be set up as under the Bennett government, but some action should be taken to correct the inequality between prices of primary and secondary products in our domestic market. We realize that the domestic market is the best market we have. Ninety-five per cent of our products, other than wheat, are consumed in the domestic market, which should be preserved for the Canadian producer and equalized as I have just suggested.
Now I come to the question of wheat and wheat marketing. Never has the western producer of wheat been in a more precarious position; never have the world wheat markets been more demoralized; never has the future looked more uncertain than is the case at the present time. After listening to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) the other day I think everyone will agree with that. We only need to look at the comments which appear in the press every day, in any paper you may pick up, to realize the truth of that statement. I would refer to the conference that took place in the city of Winnipeg not long ago, called by the premier of Manitoba, attended by representatives of the federal and provincial government, of the grain exchange, the wheat growers, the wheat pool and so on, to consider this question of the marketing of wheat. No constructive suggestion came from that conference. Then we had the international conference not long ago in London. Nothing of very much importance came from that except the appointment of a committee including the representatives of ten nations to consider five distinct subjects and report at a world conference to be held later. The fifth subject was important; it concerned the desirability of a
The Address-Mr. Perley

set export quota, not on a bushelage basis but on the basis of a percentage of world demand. Acreage reduction was definitely shelved at that meeting.
I believe that is an important subject, which should be considered. The farmers of western Canada realize now that there must be some control of production, or at least some control of marketing. I am not in favour of controlling acreage, but if I had the opportunity I think I could work out a scheme for controlling deliveries to the market. I had another resolution ready for the order paper-I do not suppose it will be reached this session-to the effect that the government should consider the advisability of amending the Canada Wheat Board Act to empower the board to control deliveries to it through a system of licensing producers to sell or deliver a given number of bushels per seeded acre, and that the permits to sell should be negotiable among the producers only. I should like to enlarge upon that matter, but time will not permit. However, I do think a system of that kind could be worked out, which would control the amount marketed based on world requirements or possible Canadian exports.
May I say here, Mr. Speaker, that I think there is altogether too much publicity given this question, altogether too much talk with respect to our difficulties in connection with marketing, too much advertising as to our surpluses, and so on. I think there should be some censorship. I hold in my hand a little chart which came to my hand just a day or two ago; I think every member received a copy of it, and I would commend it to the study of hon. gentlemen. It deals with the world and Canadian wheat situation under three heads; world and Canadian production, world and Canadian surplus and world and Canadian exports. After reviewing that, sir, I have no hesitation in saying that I am not fearful of the future. I am not a pessimist, and on that I agree with what was said by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) yesterday. I think many of these problems could and should be approached from an optimistic rather than a pessimistic point of view, and I am an optimist in connection with the possibilities of marketing our wheat in the future.
Now, I should like to say just a word with regard to the wheat board in 1938. I commend the government for carrying on that board for the 1938 crop. They set the price at 80 cents. I think if they had pursued a proper selling policy they could have set the price at 90 cents without incurring any greater loss than will be incurred under present conditions. The policy which was announced when

that price was set tended to depress the market. I have before me a statement by Mr. Sanford Evans of Winnipeg, who is a statistician of some renown, as follows:
In announcing the plan this season the government went to questionable extremes in disavowing market-price motives.
In another article Mr. Evans quotes from the Chicago Journal of Commerce, in which that newspaper said that when the price was set and the policy of the government announced, it had the effect of depressing the market. Then he quotes from Broomhall's Corn Trade News, of Liverpool, a day or two after the price was set. That should be an authority, and here is what Broomhall said:
As a fact, after a small advance, Winnipeg futures dropped several cents a bushel, considerable importance being given to a statement by the Canadian premier, Mr. Mackenzie King, that the wheat board's policy would not be to withhold supplies from the international market, but rather to offer competition at all times. In other words, no attempt is to be made to dictate prices to consumers and, in the prosecution of this policy, the government is prepared to absorb any loss which may be sustained.
The Minister of Agriculture made a very great mistake a few days after the price was set- I am not sure of the exact date-when down in Ontario he made the statement that the board was prepared to take a $30,000,000 loss. I would ask this question of any man who has had anything to do with industry:	If you had a new manager in
charge; if you had a year's business to transact, and if in the first three weeks your chief director went out telling the people to whom you expected to sell your goods that you were prepared to take a $30,000,000 loss, what would you think? I say that statement, or any statement with respect to the possible loss, should have been withheld until the last three weeks of the crop year, at least. I have already quoted statements to show that the policy as announced by the government had a depressing effect on the market.
Just here I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), one question, though it may be a question which should be placed on the order paper. Before the price was set, on August 4, did the board sell futures? Perhaps he can turn that question over in his mind and answer it some time later. The price at that time in the open market was 86 cents, and if the board did sell futures-and I hope they did- they may make a handsome profit. If that is the case we will not have the loss everyone seems to expect.
What I want to know is this: What is to be the policy of this government with respect

The Address-Mr. Perley
to the marketing of wheat in 1939? They should have a policy, and it should be announced. Western Canada was expecting that announcement by the Minister of Agriculture at the first opportunity. Does any hon. member of this house know the government policy? I do not think so. But I believe the minister has a policy. He took part in the Brandon by-election campaign, during which he spoke at Reston on October 25. He is reported by the Canadian Press as follows:
The minister stated that the government's experience with the present wheat board had convinced him that the hoard was only effective to deal with temporary emergencies.
The following day he spoke at Souris, and in the Regina Leader-Post I find the following headline:
Permanent Wheat Board Inadvisable, Gardiner Believes
It is true that a day or two later, at Saskatoon, the minister tried to correct that statement and said he did not mean exactly what the press had reported him as having said, but he can tell us now, in this house, exactly what he means; that is what we expected him to do the other day. I do believe, however, that the minister has made up his mind and that he has a policy. I would refer to the Regina Leader-Post of January 19, which I saw in the reading room the other morning. There I found this headline:
Gardiner Informally Approves of Wheat Quota Plan Proposed by Weyburn Farmer
The article goes on to say that a Mr. Lowery, of the Weyburn district, had outlined a scheme under which a farmer would be permitted to sell a thousand bushels at a dollar a bushel, and that the farmer must have been actually farming during 1938 and 1939 in order to come under the plan. The remainder of his crop could be disposed of in some other way, or through the open market. It goes on to say that the person in question had outlined the scheme, had sent it to the Minister of Agriculture and that the minister had replied saying that he informally approved of the scheme. That is the quotation from the Regina Leader-Post.

statement that the minister made a reply and that he has some policy. We would like to know what it is.
The other day the Minister of Agriculture made some observations concerning increases in acreage. His statement was that the importing countries in Europe had not increased their acreage but had improved their system of farming and had thereby increased their production. My reply to that is that Canadian producers have very materially increased their acreage in the period mentioned by the minister, but that increase in acreage was a patriotic duty. During the last one or two years of the war, and in years following, Great Britain asked Canada to make sure of a food supply for the British isles, and with that end in view we increased our acreage in western Canada for the production of wheat. That action was taken as a patriotic duty. Because of action taken at that time we find ourselves in a difficult position to-day, and I do not think that it is fair to ask the farmer to reduce his acreage, when there should be some other way of giving him a fair deal.
The minister referred to the increase of production in European countries. He might have added that Germany, Italy and France increased duties against Canadian wheat during the period between the years 1922 and 1930 when the Liberal party was in office. For the information of hon. members who are of the opinion that a general reduction in tariff to those countries means-an increase in what they purchase from us, I should like to set out certain facts. In 1922, when hon. members opposite were in office, France was enforcing a duty of 20 cents per bushel on wheat; it was admitted free into Germany and free into Italy. When the Liberal party left office in 1930, France had increased her duty to 85 cents per bushel, Germany had imposed a duty of 97 cents and Italy one of 86 cents. That was the reply made by those countries in connection with our exports of Canadian wheat, and during a period when we had made genera] reductions in rates of duties on goods coming from those parts of the world.
The Minister of Agriculture has made reference to the six-cent preference. His statement was that the removal of the preference had nothing to do with shipments through Canadian ports. May I point out that while the preference has been taken off, the United States has not offered us any compensation by reducing the duty of 42 cents on Canadian wheat entering that country. The rate still prevails. And with reference to the observation that the six-cent preference has nothing to do with grain entering through Canadian ports I would refer the minister to a statement

Under the influence of the world economic depression and the establishment of an import duty in 1932 '(with empire wheat remaining duty free), imports of United States wheat into the United Kingdom dropped from 39,267,000 bushels in 1930 (20T per cent of total wheat imports) to only 9,000 bushels in 1933 (less than -05 per cent of the total while imports from empire sources for the corresponding year rose from 79.234,000 bushels (40-5 per cent of total wheat imports) to 140,459,000 bushels (67 per cent of the total).
It is also pointed out that the United States is likely to get back business for her ports.
Then, there is something further I should like to place before the Minister of Agriculture for explanation. This is from a report in the New York Journal of Commerce, dated December 13, 1938:
Britain takes More U.S.' Subsidy Wheat 5,000,000 bushels Bought-Attainment of Export Goal is Seen
Another substantial portion of the self-imposed wheat export quota of 100,000,000 bushels for the United States has been filled with the disclosure by the Department of Agriculture late yesterday of an additional sale of 5,000,000 bushels to the United Kingdom.

Price again was not mentioned. The trade is aware, however, that low levels must have been received in view- of the depressed condition

of the world wheat market. This, in turn, means additional expensive subsidizing of the exports.
May I now refer to the matter of low prices? On my way to Ottawa I paid a visit to the grain exchange. Although I am not very popular at that place I made a call and was told that in the first sale of 20,000,000 bushels made by the United States to Great Britain under the new arrangement the market had broken to the extent of two cents, and that there had been dumping. In the agreement of 1932 with the United Kingdom there was a clause which protected the Canadian wheat grower against unfair competition, in that British authorities agreed to impose the dumping duty against Russia, the Argentine or any other country guilty of dumping. The United States has been guilty of dumping on the first sale it has made. I know the British authorities were disappointed in the fact that the market was broken to the extent of two cents. The British producer is subsidized in his own market to the extent of SI .30 per bushel. Every cent the Liverpool market is broken is another cent out of the British treasury.
As the time at my disposal is drawing to a close there are some matters with which I shall not have time to deal. I wish however to refer briefly to the treaty. From the standpoint of increased export trade I do not believe the results will be satisfactory. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) admitted giving concessions but he did not give details of compensations we were to receive. He is trying to sell the idea to the primary producers of Canada that he is giving up preferences as a means of promoting harmony, unity and peace. What bunk! I do not believe the western producer will swallow that explanation. He will not believe that it is necessary for us to give up all these preferences in order to create peace and unity among the English-speaking nations or democracies. Does the Prime Minister think the United States would not want our friendship if Japan happened to throw a few bombs in the country across the border? What does the Prime Minister think of what Hitler will say with respect to the fact that we have foregone our six-cent preference? Will he be more friendly to us? There is nothing assured in the treaty.
I have made some calculation with respect to the quota on live stock, and they show that the constituency of Qu'Appelle could supply a very considerable proportion of the quota, and four times the milk quota.

In conclusion I wish to point out that the British market is the stable market of the world. During the whole period of the depression Great Britain decreased her exports by only five per cent, whereas the exports of France decreased 56 per cent, of Germany 77 per cent and of Italy 60 per cent. I urge that these figures prove the assertion that Great Britain is the stable market-and we are now out of it.
I asked the minister a few moments ago to state the wheat policy of the government, and I hope that he or some other member of the cabinet will do so. Why was industry not consulted in the making of this agreement? Why did not this parliament have the opportunity to pass on it, as it had in 1932? All that western Canada wants is a square deal. There is no east or west so far as we are concerned, and I regret to see that some of the press are trying to make an issue of that. The Conservative party intends to give the west a square deal. Ours will be a constructive policy that will give protection to the great agricultural industry of the west, the backbone of this dominion; and the Conservative party realizes that just as well as anyone else.
Just a word with respect to the subamendment. In great part I could have supported it, but I regret that I am unable to do so because of the way it is worded. If the amendment had read "those financial institutions which are exploiting the Canadian people" I would gladly have supported it. But we have a certain control over financial institutions generally at the present time. I would be almost one hundred per cent, I was going to say, behind the subamendment if there had been one other word in it. As it is I propose to support the amendment of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), and I shall have something further to say later as important problems come before the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on this the first occasion of my addressing this house, recognizing my obligation to the city of Victoria, the constituency which I am proud to represent here. I recognize also my obligation to hon. members to make any suggestions that I con-71 492-l8i
sider will tend to create a better understanding between the different parts of Canada and better conditions within our country.
I would ask the house to bear with me for a moment while I say a word about the city of Victoria. I believe that its advantages are fully appreciated, generally speaking, but in some quarters our city is not very well known. I shall not say anything about its wonderful climate or about the beauty of the city itself. I do not wish to say anything in particular about our industries, which are mainly lumbering, mining and fishing, and the tourist trade. But I do wish to say a word about Victoria as the western gateway to Canada. It is the gateway to Canada for all those people who are living on the shores of the Pacific ocean, and as such the city of Victoria and its citizens recognize their responsibility to the rest of Canada. We would like to make it such a city that when people enter it for the first time they will get not only a view of the beauty of the city itself but a glimpse into the character of the people who live in this wonderful country of Canada.
I am sorry to say, however, that we have at least one drawback in Victoria. Our outer port is very badly run down, and is very greatly in need of repair. It presents a very bad approach to the city. It is owned practically by the dominion government, and I am in hopes, Mr. Speaker, that the present condition will be improved within a short time.
I should like now to join with other members in congratulating the mover (Mr. Matthews) and the seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I had never before had the experience of listening to addresses of this kind, but from what has already been said by so many members of the outstanding ability of the mover and the seconder, I can readily understand that their rank with other speakers on similar occasions is very high. I heartily congratulate them both upon their efforts.
I should like now to refer briefly but most sincerely to the forthcoming visit of our king and queen to Canada, and particularly to their visit to the city of Victoria. I can assure hon. gentlemen that the kindness and warmth of the reception which their majesties will receive in the city of Victoria will not be surpassed by that of any other community of equal size in this dominion. I am pleased to note that a representative has already left Ottawa and spent a week-end in Victoria arranging for their majesties' visit. Already offers of assistance are coming in from all quarters of the city and from people
The Address-Mr. Mayhem

in all walks of life who are anxious to assist in the reception. I hope that a definite organization will soon get under way to coordinate the efforts of those who are willing to assist in the reception, and that everybody, particularly our young people, will be given the opportunity to see their king and queen.
The benefits that will accrue from this visit will be many, and I hope they will be permanent. I hope that it will be a time when we as the people of Canada will examine our own hearts and minds and find out for ourselves if we are big enough to look beyond the boundaries of our own community, over the borders of our own province, and beyond the shores of our own country and realize that we are an integral part of the British Empire, and that as such we have a right and a duty to stand with the empire in peace or in war, for good or for ill.
As a new member and comparative stranger in the house, Mr. Speaker, it would not be in veiy good taste for me to criticize men who are much my senior in matters of government, men who I am sure are just as sincere as I am and who will do all they can to make a contribution to the welfare and progress of Canada. But I cannot refrain from remarking that much of the criticism which has been offered by the opposition has been about as original and as constructive and as annoying as losing one's gate on Hallowe'en. This "do-nothing government" is a phrase coined for election purposes, and it is no more reliable than catchwords and slogans often are. I am inclined to believe that the people of Canada read the reports of proceedings in this house, and I am sure that we can depend on their intelligence.
Much has been said in this debate about the diminution of trade in Canada. It is true there has been a diminution, but is the government responsible for that? Is not the diminution of trade due to world conditions? Has not trade diminished because countries are at war with one another, while other countries are engaged in preparation for war?
Mention has been made in this debate particularly of the pulp and paper industry. I happen to have been engaged in that industry for the last twenty-four years, and I admit that the pulp and paper industry on the Pacific coast is having a hard struggle at the present time, but that is not due to any action by this government. It is due particularly to the war between China and Japan. Some of our trouble in the lumber industry is also due to similar conditions.

I am inclined to think that, rather than criticize the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), we should compliment him on the interest that he has taken in world affairs. I am confident that in taking that interest he will help to correct the present situation. I am confident that, with the new trade agreement in effect, with things settled in the orient and in Europe, we shall not be looking for a solution of our unemployed problem; the difficulty will be rather the other way, namely to find men able to do the work. I am sorry to see evidence in so many places of defeatism in our people. Even at the present time in some of our cities we have no great surplus of trained mechanics. The wastage of ten years will have to be taken care of. Let the clouds of war roll by, give us a few years of peace, and we shall soon find a solution of the problem of unemployment.
My attitude to the tripartite trade agreement is one of gratification, appreciation and general satisfaction. I do not believe that the people of Canada are looking for a gift in the way of trade; they are looking for an equitable agreement, because they realize that it must be equitable to endure. We are looking not for a good bargain but for an opportunity to trade beneficially and uninterruptedly on a friendly basis. We are not looking for a one-way street, as some would indicate. Yet in fairness one must admit that there is a little hardship in some branches of both industry and agriculture. I will mention one branch of agriculture that is affected, particularly in our own district -potato growing. Before the present agreement went into effect the potato grower had the privilege of a countervailing duty which he does not now enjoy. That countervailing privilege was given to him by the present government in the agreement of 1936. He has enjoyed it for two years; but he is no worse off than he was before that time. On the other hand ihe agriculturist reaps a benefit from the sale of his cattle, his hogs, his dairy products, and many other items, as well as getting an advantage on the things which he has to purchase.
There has been some criticism in this house because of the loss of the six-cent preference on wheat. Naturally we would have liked to see it retained, but I believe the change will provide at least one advantage which we cannot overlook. Wheat, after all, is a raw material. Will not the effect be to encourage the milling business in our country?-and if that happens, the by-products from that milling business will go a long way towards the raising of cheaper cattle and cheaper hogs. It will at least provide cheaper food for our live stock.

The Address-Mr. Mayhew
One branch of the lumbering industry which is particularly pleased with the treaty is the cedar shingle business. We have several such firms and factories in Victoria. Not only is their quota increased but they are able to continue to sell on a comparatively small duty after their quota has been filled. The lumber business generally is not finding fault with the treaty. Naturally retailers would have liked to retain the full British preference, but they realize in fairness they have to give something. They realize also that the value of a trade with 130,000,000 people across an imaginary boundary line, without any transportation difficulties, is far greater than a market of probably fifty million people six thousand miles away, with transportation interferences to be overcome.
Just here I should like to say a word as to how we may counteract some of the disadvantages that we are under in the way of trade, if we are prepared to pay the price. Alberta is full of coal. Why not bring some of it from Alberta to the east and keep our men in Alberta and the employees of the railways busy, rather than buy our coal from the other side? I ask further, why not bring petroleum products from the Alberta oil fields and use them down here rather than purchase our gasoline and fuel from the other side? Why not give a little assistance to our moving picture industry at the coast, so that we may be able to use our own pictures rather than buy them from the other side? There are many ways in which we can assist, provided we are prepared to pay the bill.
I wish to deal for a moment or two with the youth problem and with youth training. I do not suppose there is a man in this house possessing any of the milk of human kindness who will not be interested in assistance to our youth. I believe the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) should be thanked for what he has done, and encouraged in his work. I cannot understand how the opposition can be honest and yet call the government a do-nothing government when they consider what has been done for youth and for the cure of unemployment. The government is to be congratulated on the start it has made upon the training of youth in Canada. It is true that it is only a start, but reports coming in from every province, such as we had the opportunity of hearing the other night, are evidence that that start is appreciated by the mothers and fathers of the young people of this country.
We talk a great deal about the wonderful natural resources of Canada, but of all the potential values in Canada there is nothing to be compared with the potential value of oui
young people, and I urge that we give them every opportunity we can to make full use of their Canadian citizenship.
Large numbers of high school graduates, as well as those who do not complete a high school course, cannot find jobs. More and more, the young people reaching the age of employment each year encounter a regiment of newly-invented machines, competing with them for their jobs.
The failure to keep the open door of opportunity for youth is tantamount to recruiting large numbers for the marching clubs of dictators. Since this condition is a serious one is it not time to stop criticizing the efforts that are being put forth, and to make suggestions that may help, viewing every suggestion with an open mind in the hope that out of it all some good may come?
We must not create the impression that the government owes a living to our young people. The government does owe the young people good sound practical education and as little interference as possible so that they as individuals may develop themselves and our natural resources. We do owe them an opportunity to make a living, but the obligation on the part of the government is particularly that of education. That I think we are doing in the youth training program. I would like to see it extended so as to give all young men who have left school and who are unable to find employment three chances -in fact I would say four. It would have to be on a purely voluntary basis, and the choice would have to be theirs. The opportunities I would suggest are these; that they be given an opportunity of joining the militia; that they be given an opportunity of joining the navy, and that this government establish training farms where they may learn agriculture. These farms could be small units scattered through the provinces so that the men trained on them would be absorbed in their own communities as soon as the training had been completed. The other suggestion I make is that mercantile marine training ships be established on both the Atlantic and the Pacific. Many of our boys to-day are jumping into ships, going off to learn seamanship without realizing the nobility of the profession, without realizing the dangers and hazards of it. The result is that after one or two trips they find they are not fitted for the calling. A few weeks in foreign ports is enough to ruin the boy himself. If he were put on a training ship under a proper man he would appreciate the responsibilities of the profession and such training would make him a good mercantile mariner.
The Address-Mr. Mayhew

With regard to the other two suggestions, I believe that this government have the facilities as well as men of calibre, intellect, loyalty and ability, men who could direct boys in both the militia and the navy, giving them a chance to learn a vocation under reasonable discipline.
I should like to add a further suggestion to the one I have already made. It has to do with the treatment of our older people, because the youth of to-day will be the elderly people of to-morrow. I believe that there is no fear in the human mind so great, no fear that retards the activities and efforts of people to the same extent, as the fear that when one is old one will be dependent upon friends or the government for a living. That fear, I believe, can be very largely banished by putting into effect a compulsory contributory superannuation policy. By this I mean that all employers and all employees in any walk of life should be obliged to contribute an equal share so as to provide for the superannuation of employees when they have reached the age of sixty or sixty-five. I am sure that there would be no opposition to a policy of this kind from the larger employers of labour, and I do not believe that there would be any objection to it by labour itself. It is not fair either to the people or to the government of Canada that workers at the zenith of their earning capacity should be allowed to drift on without making adequate provision for their needs when they are unable to work. Nor is it fair for the employer to use the best part of a life of the employee, making use of him in a competitive system, and then when he is worn out toss him on the scrap heap without consideration as one would a piece of worn out machinery. The government's contribution to this scheme would be one of management, to see to it that the funds as they were collected were properly taken care of.
I would suggest that a uniform plan for Canada be proposed by the dominion government, but that each province look after its own collections, investing its funds in its own securities with the endorsement of the federal government, and thus giving the fund raised for this purpose every security possible. Could we in any saner or better way repatriate our government loans than through some subh mode of procedure?
In conclusion I wish to thank the government for what it has been able to do: the consummation of the United States trade agreement; its contribution to unemployment and relief; its. contribution to unemployment through the home improvement plan-and in this regard I would ask whether this plan could be extended to business properties so

that many of the present dilapidated buildings in our cities might be improved; its contribution to home life through the home building plan; its contribution to people living in municipalities through its municipal aid plan. I would ask the government to pursue this policy of progress so vigorously that no reasonable member could stand in this house and accuse it of being static.
As a business man I think the only definite cure for our present trouble is an expanding policy. I admit that there is a danger of expanding too rapidly, and in my opinion the expansion of business must not be left entirely to the government. It is an obligation on the part of the individual as well. It is an obligation put upon us by democracy and must be carried out if we are to retain that privilege. In a word, I believe that industry, not quack remedy, is the solution of our present distressing problems.

speechtext:
May I join with those who have preceded me in extending congratulations to the mover (Mr. Matthews) and the seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I was particularly pleased to listen to the mover of the motion because I had the pleasure of knowing him and his family in Brandon some years ago when I attended college there. It was a very' great pleasure for me to hear him make such a fine impression in his maiden speech in this house. I should like also to extend my congratulations to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) upon his accession to his new and difficult position. He is following in the footsteps of a gifted and able predecessor, and I trust he will be granted strength to discharge the duties of his office in a manner that will bring credit to himself and the Dominion of Canada.
I am sorry I cannot concur with hon. members opposite in lauding the pact of Munich as a milestone on the road to world peace. In my opinion, the pact of Munich did not avert war; it only postponed war until that time when, collective action having become impossible, and our allies having fled, the English-speaking nations of the world, isolated and discredited, will face the fascist aggressors alone. The pact of Munich was the final culmination of a long series of concessions to force, each concession leading to a situation that demanded still further surrender. Yielding to dictators does not bring peace; it merely brings about demands for further concessions. However, it is not my purpose at this time to discuss the question of foreign policy, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) having assured the house

The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
that ample opportunity will later on be afforded for a discussion of the matter. Neither do I wish to discuss the government's announcement that there will be increased expenditure for national defence, because that, too, will be debated later in the session. I do wish, however, to urge upon the government that before they bring down the estimates for increased expenditures for national defence, they shall first of all bring down legislation dealing with the national control of the armament industry.

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that democracy is on trial to-day as it has not been on trial for centuries. I believe that democracy must be made to work, and that unless it can provide jobs for the unemployed, equitable prices for the farmers, and give opportunities and stability to the business and professional classes, democracy will be thrust aside in favour of some other form of government. It is not enough to talk about democracy. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has talked more about democracy than any other

The Address-Mr. McNevin
man in Canada, and perhaps, in view of his great opportunity, he has done less than any other man in Canada to preserve it.
The Prime Minister also talks about national unity. But people do not unite simply because you tell them to unite. People unite if they have some great goal in common, and when they feel they are marching toward some national attainment, with some unity of purpose. But the people of Canada do not believe they are marching towards some national attainment.
We in this group believe in democracy. But by democracy we do not mean laissez-faire, maintaining things as they are, inefficiency. We believe that you can have freedom and social security; we believe that you can have democracy and employment. We believe that you can have liberty and economic planning; we believe that we can give to the people of Canada a more abundant life without destroying freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, freedom of the press, freedom of religion, or parliamentary institutions. Rather we believe that building upon these fundamentals of our society we can go forward from political democracy to economic democracy, without which all talk of democracy is idle and futile.
Abraham Lincoln said that no nation could long exist half-slave and half-free. It is equally true that no nation can long exist politically free and economically enslaved. That is where we part company with hon. gentlemen opposite. I believe that most of them are democrats but they are political democrats, not social democrats, not economic democrats. They believe that parliament should be controlled by the people of Canada, but that the economic life of Canada should be left in the hands of the monopolies and financial barons. But unless parliament is prepared to control big business, in a few years big business will control parliament. That has happened in other countries, and it can happen here.
We in this group believe that the salvation of Canada depends upon this parliament taking effective steps to control those financial institutions and monopolistic enterprises that are now exploiting the people of Canada. When we have done that, and only when we have done that, can we be sure that government of the people, for the people and by the people shall not perish from the earth.

Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose first of all of extending my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Matthews) and the seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address to his excellency in reply to the speech from the throne. Both hon. members made a profound impression upon this assembly.
My next thought is to express great pleasure and satisfaction on my part and on the part of my constituents at the proposed visit of Their Majesties the King and Queen to this dominion in the months of May and June. This gracious gesture on the part of our sovereigns, which is without precedent in our history, will I am sure quicken the spirit of loyalty within the mind and heart of every true Canadian.
As one of the members who did not have the pleasure prior to the present session of parliament of sitting in the house with the hon. member for London, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), I desire to extend to him my heartiest congratulations upon being chosen to lead his party. May I also express my sincere wish that he may long be spared to lead His Majesty's Loyal Opposition in this dominion.
I wish to voice a note of regret at the retirement of one of the foremost privy councillors in the history of this parliament. I refer to the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Elliott), the former Postmaster General. Mr. Elliott has had a long and distinguished public career in the public life of his native province and in that of this dominion.
I feel I should be remiss in my duty if I did not add a word of congratulations to the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. McLarty) and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. MacKinnon) who have been chosen to take their places on the front benches of the government. I go a step further than the other hon. members who have preceded me; I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the government upon being able to secure the services of these two gentlemen, who I am sure are well qualified for the strenuous duties that have been assigned to them.
During the course of this debate much has been said upon the questions referred to in the speech from the throne, and not a little has been said upon matters untouched or unmentioned in the speech. This is in accordance with the usual custom, but in the course of my remarks I shall endeavour, with a few exceptions, to confine myself to the subject matters contained in the speech itself.
The first question which I wish to discuss is marketing. It is a very large question, and for the present I shall content myself with making a few observations with regard to the wheat situation. At the very outset I want to make it perfectly clear that I am not going to offer serious objection to the action taken by the government in setting the price of wheat at eighty cents a bushel for the crop year of 1938. In the year 1937 I
The Address-Mr. McNevin

travelled over a large part of the drought area in western Canada. I am therefore, in a position to judge with regard to conditions existing on the prairies at that time. However, I feel sure there will be general assent to the suggestion that we cannot establish as a settled policy in our economy provisions which would permit the payment of a set price for any commodity in one part of Canada and deny the same concession to those producing a similar commodity in other parts of the country. In addition, may I point to the unequal results which must inevitably follow the distribution of funds on the basis referred to, that is the eighty cent price for western wheat. For example, to the farmers' who have much, much is given; to the farmers who have little, little is given; and to the farmers who have nothing, nothing is given.
Furthermore, may I point to what I believe would be a dangerous precedent. For instance, supposing a large producer delivered under this plan ten, twenty, or even thirty thousand bushels of wheat-which I assume is not impossible-and the world price eventually turned out to be twenty cents below the set price, the thirty thousand bushel producer under these circumstances would receive from the federal treasury $6,000 on one year's operations. I am of opinion that the significance of this statement requires no further comment.
Then we have the broad aspect of the situation to consider. Is it practicable to select one particular commodity and set the price for it, thus ignoring the producers of other commodities which may entail as much or more effort and expense to produce? Upon this aspect of the question I may have some further remarks to make at some future time.
Now let us analyze some of the conditions affecting the marketing of wheat. We have in one classification the exporting countries and in another classification the importing countries, in regard to this commodity. A review of the figures of the importing countries for the last five years, 1933-1938, shows that wheat imports were on the average for that five-year period 223,000,000 bushels less than the average during the 1922-1927 period. What is taking place is that coarse grains, potato flour, rice flour, chemicals, et cetera, are replacing wheat flour on the tables of the consumers in these countries. It is true that these substitutes are much inferior to wheat flour; therefore this changed condition represents a lowering of the standard of living in the countries referred to. Some of these countries may not be in a position to purchase both bullets
[Mr. McNevin.)
and bread. The purchase of the latter is restricted and the purchase of materials for the former is increased. The net result is to increase the surplus of exporting countries, of which Canada is one of the greatest, and thereby reduce world prices for wheat.
Now with respect to the Ontario farmers' position, the increased price in some lines of production has improved their position over a few years ago. I believe the majority of the farmers referred to have been able in the last three or four years to meet their immediate obligations. Complete recovery has been impossible, due to the accumulation of unpaid taxes, unpaid interest, repairs which should have been made but were not, worn-out equipment which should have been replaced but was not-all of which was piling up for the previous five or six years. I have no hesitation in saying that the Ontario farmer is not in a financial position to assist in carrying the burden of taxation which would be necessary to maintain permanent fixed prices which must be materially above world prices for any farm commodity in other parts of the country. The whole question of set prices for farm products will be under consideration later in the session, when all aspects of the situation must be fully explored.
With reference to the problems of unemployment and relief: both of these difficult questions are in a large measure attributable to the low price level of farm products. I venture to predict that, in spite of palliative measures which may be used, no permanent solution will be achieved with regard to these matters until such time that farmers' returns are comparable with those of people who are engaged in other important vocations. If this were attained, it would immediately reflect an improvement in the position of the low wage employee.
In view of the remarks made by some hon. members to my immediate left with respect to employment in industry and with respect to the effect of the trade policies o( this government upon improvement in industry in this country, that is the next point which I desire to discuss for a few minutes.
I am of opinion that our greatest problem is the surplus of unskilled labour. I so state because a review of employment by industries shows that while employment is down slightly when compared with 1937, it represents a substantial improvement over any other year since 1930. In fact it is only surpassed in the years 1929 and 1930 since the post war period. The figures I now propose to place upon Hansard cover employment in manufacturing, logging, mining, communication, transportation, construction, service and trade. The reason I

I am not one to state that all our economic troubles in the depression years were caused by the government policies in force at that time. I believe the policy of economic nationalism which was pursued by the government of that day was one of the important contributing factors in connection with our
The Address-Mr. McNevin
economic troubles. At the present time I give some credit to the trade and other policies of the present government as a means of assisting to counteract a contraction in industry and business comparable with the extreme condition of unemployment which prevailed for many months in the neighbouring country to the south, the United States.
I think this is a splendid example and endorsation of the policies of this government which have materially assisted stability in Canada, and I make this comparison with regard to employment in the United States and employment in Canada. A comparison between these two countries for the years 1937 and 1938 shows a drop in industry in Canada of approximately three per cent, while in the United States for a similar period the drop amounted to slightly over nineteen per cent. In this connection may I point out what must be firmly impressed on the minds of all the members of this house, that government spending on a huge scale does not cure economic ills nor offer any permanent cure for unemployment. For this reason I trust that as the discussions of this session proceed, the interests of the taxpayer will receive more recognition and consideration by this parliament than has been the case so far in this debate.
I come now to an item which is of special interest and significance to myself and my constituency. I refer to that portion of the speech from the throne dealing with matters pertaining to the Department of National Defence. I so state because dominion arsenal No. 2 is located in the riding I have the honour to represent. Before proceeding further, I desire to convey to the minister of this department my appreciation of the start which is under way at the Lindsay arsenal; but this represents but a small part of the plant. It is a well-established fact that the administration which preceded us prepared plans and already had proceeded with the construction of additional extensive arsenal buildings at Valcartier.
As is well known to the officials of the government, soon after my entry into this parliament I offered strenuous objection to this development because it appeared unreasonable to me to proceed with the construction of additional arsenal buildings to meet the needs of this department when at the same time the extensive facilities at Lindsay were idle and unused except for storage purposes. I am well aware that until that time the Lindsay arsenal had been classified as an auxiliary arsenal for use when the country was actually engaged in war. I also
The Address-Mr. McNevin

offered my strenuous objection to this policy. It is true that during the regime of our predecessors, and up to the present time, certain requirements of the department were procured from private industry on the basis of cost plus profit. Mr. Speaker, I want to make my position perfectly clear with regard to this point. I am unalterably opposed to the further extension of this policy until such time as all the remaining facilities for production at the Lindsay arsenal have been utilized. I strongly favour and urge upon the government and this parliament the policy of using the government arsenals to their utmost capacity when it is necessary in times of peace. With respect to private industry it should stand ready in times of war for auxiliary armament production. At such times the interests of the Canadian people should be carefully safeguarded by government supervision of such plants. Now, having so expressed myself, I trust that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) whom I, in common with the large majority of Canadian people, hold in very high esteem, will, when the opportunity presents itself, inform the house in regard to the government's intentions with respect to this important matter.
I come now to another point. In listening to the addresses of hon. members to my immediate left, I note but little variation in their remarks. The thought occurred to me that the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) may have missed his calling in taking up medicine. He should have been a schoolmaster, because it would appear that his followers, in the absence of any reasonable grounds upon which to attack the administration, have learned to repeat a few inapplicable phrases, prominent among which we find the one, "do-nothing government". I say, let the opposition be fair. If we look out upon the world around us to the south, to the east, or to the west, do we find the sun of tranquillity, of prosperity, of peace and contentment, shining with its noonday strength upon the nations? I feel sorry that it is not so. But what do we see? War, and the rumblings and rumours of war. In many lands when the sun goes down the people know not what the morning may bring forth. This condition resembles very much, in fact it is in some respects more aggravated than, the condition behind which these same hon. members excuse their own inaction.
* This government has diligently applied itself to the difficult problems confronting it, and has more definite accomplishments to its credit than any other government since confederation. What are they? In the first place,

with respect to exploring world markets, more effective trade agreements have been negotiated by this government than by any of its predecessors. I mention this point particularly because it has a quite definite interest to farmers, lumbermen, and others in my own constituency. Under the provisions of the 1935 treaty, lumber producers, live stock producers, and producers in various other lines of agriculture have received great benefits. In fact, I sometimes wonder, if it had not been for that assistance, where the live stock producers and others would be at the present time. Furthermore, the final completion of the revision of that treaty, which will be before the house in the not distant future, contains in my opinion many provisions which will much more adequately serve the interests of the Canadian people.
In my riding there is a large woollen manufacturing industry. I observe in the provisions of the Great Britain-United States treaty that the woollen industry of Great Britain has been given material concessions upon woollen textiles entering the United States. Canada is not mentioned; that provision deals only with the nation which in connection with the exchange of commodities contributes the largest quota of the article, but the same provision applies to Canada. I am satisfied that the woollen textile industry in Canada will reap substantial benefit from the treaty reductions on woollen goods entering the United States.
The recent pronouncement by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) regarding the problem of transients deals with an extremely difficult situation. I am sure every hon. member has great sympathy for the transients. I pay tribute to the thousands of Canadian citizens who, while not working at the present time, are willing and anxious to work. But the principle embodied in the British legislation should apply, whereby men, when given the opportunity to work, must accept that work in preference to relief. In saying this, however, I do not mean that married men should be removed from their homes and families.
I might proceed to enumerate many more accomplishments of this government:	for
example, the taking over of the central bank. When this government assumed office, credit was hard to get from banks, while to-day the banks are looking for borrowers who have any reasonable security. We have also the housing legislation; the elimination of taxation on the construction industry; and a constructive youth training program is under way. I do not know what form the government expenditures through the Department of Labour may

The Address-Mr. Sewn
take. If the construction of the trans-Canada highway is resumed, I would be interested in seeing it completed through the eastern section of northern Ontario, and I should like to see an artery built through Algonquin park, which is in my riding. Our citizens and tourists would then have the opportunity of travelling north and south as well as east and west. But that matter will come up for discussion later on. I know that up to a certain point road problems are entirely provincial matters. The latest proposal to absorb a larger share of relief costs will greatly relieve the excessive taxation on real estate, and act as a stimulant to business and the building trade.
Then with regard to national defence: what were the conditions when this government came into power? A group of officers and men equal to those of any other country were training with antiquated and obsolete equipment. Now we have modern aeroplanes-

In answer to the contention that this is a do-nothing government, I simply say that they have proceeded along sane lines, acting on the motto that where there is a will there is a way.
