speechtext:
As this debate proceeds it is becoming difficult to avoid repetition in discussion of the matters referred to in the speech from the throne. There is, however, one important matter which received very little attention in that speech, and which, until a day or two ago at least, has received very little comment by hon. members in the house. But it is a most important matter to all the citizens of Canada. I refer to the plight in which agriculture finds itself in this country, and I intend to confine my remarks largely to a discussion of that
question. It is true that some mention was made in the speech from the throne of the intention of the government to revise the grain act and to introduce a bill further to regulate grain exchanges. But these are matters which affect only the farmer in the west, in fact the western wheat grower, and have very little to do with the problems facing the mixed farmers of Canada. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) this afternoon made an excellent speech in discussing the problems of the western wheat growers,, but I wish to take a few minutes to discuss the problems of farmers in Ontario and particularly those engaged in mixed farming.
Before proceeding further, I should like personally and on behalf of my constituents, to join in the unanimous expressions of rejoicing in this house over the approaching visit of Their Gracious Majesties the King and Queen. Their visit will undoubtedly tend to increase the loyalty and devotion to the crown of all true Canadians, and will also tend to strengthen the ties which bind Canada to the empire.
I also wish to express the satisfaction and relief of the people of my constituency at the fact that the recent threat of war has been averted for the time being. In every municipality in the constituency of Haldimand cenotaphs have been erected bearing the names of those who made the supreme sacrifice in the great war. They serve to remind us, among other things, of the horrors of warfare. The memory of those trying days is still fresh in the minds of everyone, and I express the hope of all Canadians that any international complications which still exist may be speedily and amicably settled without recourse to arms.
I should like also to take this opportunity of expressing the pleasure I feel at the reentry into this house of the hon. member for London (Mr. Manion). I wish to congratulate him upon being chosen as leader of a great party. He possesses those qualifications, those graces of heart and of mind, which have made him an able debater and one of the most pleasant and gracious personalities in the house. I make one prediction, and it is that in the next house he will lead a much larger group than he does at present; and, unless all signs fail, I believe he will be Prime Minister.
In listening to the debate which has taken place so far, it seems to me strange that so little enthusiasm on the part of hon. members sitting on the government benches has been displayed over the new trade agreements. A survey of their speeches in Hansard will show that, apart from the mover and the seconder of the address, very little comment has been
The Address-Mr. Senn

made by hon. gentlemen opposite. This attitude is in direct contrast to the enthusiasm which was evidenced when the 1935 agreement was brought into the house. On February 25, 1936, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) introduced the resolution approving the 1935 trade agreement and used these words, as they appear at page 502 of Hansard for that year:
The government of the United States and the government of this country were actuated by one and the same motive, namely to make an agreement which would be equally beneficial to both countries. . . . Could anything destroy the agreement more effectively than that it should be shown in the course of the next three years that one country had got considerably the better of the other? Would not the effect of an agreement reached in that way be to destroy the possibility of its continuance beyond the period of three years.
The trade figures for the past few years prove conclusively that one party to the agreement, to -use the Prime Minister's words, did get considerably the better of the other, although that has not prevented the government from continuing the treaty and negotiating a new one. Let me for a moment review the question of trade balances between the two countries. The other day the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) pooh-poohed the idea that trade balances had any particular significance. The hon. member is an expert in statistics. He has always professed a great belief in the value of figures, and from time to time has used figures to prove his own arguments. I suggest that the trend of trade balances between the two countries indicates, more clearly than anything else could, the effects of the treaty of 1935 upon Canadian trade with the United States. For the first thirty years of this century Canada had an unfavourable trade balance with the United States amounting to over five and a half billion dollars. That is an enormous sum of money, much greater than our national debt if we do not take into account our railway liability. It is about five times as great as the average annual agricultural production of this country during the past ten years. Yet that does not take into account the sums of money which have been sent to the United States in payment of interest charges and dividends. That flow of money across the border has greatly retarded our progress in days gone by; it has had a very bad effect upon our industrial and economic life and also upon our population, because during those years thousands and, indeed, hundreds of thousands of our young men followed that flow of money across the border in order to obtain employment.

When the Bennett government came into power in 1930, however, one of the first acts they performed was to revise our tariff schedules, placing them almost on a level with those tariffs which the United States had raised against Canadian products. The result of that action became apparent immediately. Our unfavourable trade balance began to dwindle and finally disappeared altogether, so that in 1934, 1935 and 1936 we again had favourable trade balances with the United States amounting to some $120,000,000. When the new treaty came into effect in 1936 another change took place, and in 1937 we again had an unfavourable trade balance of some $8,000,000, which rose last year to about $79,000,000. So, if we consider the Prime Minister's statement in view of these figures, what could be more apparent than that one country did get considerably the better of the other in connection with that agreement? Yet the present government, obsessed as it is with the idea of making treaties, has entered into another agreement with the same country. It is a treaty which will give little if any encouragement to Canadian agriculture, but it will encourage the importation of manufactured goods into Canada not only from the United States but also from all those countries which are enjoying favoured nation treatment.
In the speech from the throne much attention has been paid to the question of unemployment, which continues, of course, to be one of our most pressing and urgent problems. On the other hand, as I said in the beginning of my remarks, little has been said of the problems facing agriculture, which problems are just as important and just as vital to the prosperity of Canada as any others that exist in this dominion. Perhaps little was said about the problems facing agriculture because many at least of the ministers of the crown made statements at the beginning of the year forecasting what they thought would be the situation in the country during the year to come. For a moment I should like to refer to the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), appearing in the Globe and Mail of January 3, 1939; I believe it is worthy of comment. Among other things the hon. gentleman asserted that there was an abundance of feed in Canada; that is, feed for live stock. He also made the significant statement that the numbers of our live stock -hogs, cattle and so on-had greatly decreased and on that fact he based the prediction that live stock prices probably would advance. To me it seems strange-indeed, it is a commentary upon the inaction of this

The Address-Mr. Senn
government-that the only prediction the minister made in regard to better agricultural prices was based on the fact that the numbers of our live stock had decreased. I remember very well the glowing terms the minister used some three years ago when he told the house he was going to institute a marketing branch within the department; but now, after that branch has been in operation for three years, all the minister can say is that we may have better prices for live stock simply because their numbers have decreased.
The farmer has been always faced with that very difficulty. In years of plenty prices fall, generally below the cost of production. In years of scarcity, or when the farmer has very little to sell, prices soar. In 1938 we had a bumper crop; yet prices of all kinds of grain and feed fell to the lowest level they have experienced since the very trough of the depression. It is true that in 1938 the farmers of Canada, and particularly those in the western provinces, had more difficulty in paying their taxes and meeting their obligations than they have had in many years.
I am convinced that the cure for unemployment does not lie in measures such as those advanced by the government, including the home improvement plan and the new housing plan, or in the expenditure of public moneys, such as has been forecast in the speech from the throne, for building programs to provide work. Nor do I think that the cure for unemployment lies in another suggestion made yesterday by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), namely the employment of men on our farms. I say that simply because the farmers of to-day cannot compete with other industries in the labour market.
After all, these are only palliative measures and provide no permanent employment. I believe the causes underlying unemployment in Canada are economic. To a great extent they arise from an unbalanced price structure. I do not suggest for a moment that prices of manufactured goods are too high; I do not suggest that the price of labour is too high, but I do say that the price of farm products is out of proportion to other commodity prices in this country. Recently the Hon. Mr. Morrison, Minister of Agriculture in Great Britain, speaking in the British House of Commons upon the question of the orderly marketing of farm products, concluded his remarks with these words:
I hope the lesson is now well learnt that this great edifice we have built up of commerce and industry in various countries rests upon the foundation of primary production throughout the world, the empire and our country. If the primary producer is denied his proper reward, it soon brings ruin upon those who
hope to sell him their goods, and I believe that stable organization for a market of this kind would really be a contribution not only to the prosperity of agriculture, but to the prosperity of trade and commerce as a whole throughout the world.
Those words express much more concisely than I could the idea I am trying to present. For instance, if agriculture were to be placed on a prosperous footing, it would immediately and of necessity initiate a building program much greater than any government can afford, simply because farm buildings and equipment are sadly in need of repairs and replacements, which cannot be carried out under present conditions.
It is, after all, the new wealth created each year in primary industry which maintains the buying power of the people, and which is in large measure the controlling factor of distribution. We have a number of primary industries in Canada, but the greatest of them, the greatest industry of all, is agriculture. It is therefore most important that the farmer should receive a price commensurate with the cost of his production, so that he may buy a liberal share of all kinds of merchandise. If this could be brought about, I believe our unemployment difficulties would gradually but surely disappear.
Governmental activities, both federal and provincial, have largely been directed towards assisting and teaching the farmer to produce efficiently and economically. I am not trying to discredit the operations of governments in this respect. Essential and efficient services have been performed, and the farmer has been taught the value of good live stock, good seed and proper cultivation. He has been taught soil chemistry, food values, balanced rations, and so on. But too little attention has been paid by governments and departments of agriculture to the farmers' most pressing problem, namely, the marketing of his products.
I have stated many times, in this house and in other places, that if the farmer were assured of attractive prices he would produce goods in quantity and in quality. But he has little encouragement when prices for farm products fluctuate as violently and rapidly as they are doing to-day, and as they have been doing for some time past.
Agriculture must take a leaf from the book of industry, and set up a proper system of merchandizing its products. The day is gone for the producer as an individual to market on a competitive, cutthroat, hit-or-miss basis, without knowledge of what other producers do, or what his competitors do from day to day.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
The Address-Mr. Serin

After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house
rose at six o'clock I was discussing the imperative need for more stability in the price of farm products in Canada. I had stated that if the farmer could be assured of prices which were commensurate with the cost of efficient production, our unemployment problem would gradually disappear. It cannot be questioned that farm prices are not on a parity with those of other commodities, particularly in times of plentiful production on the farm. The reasons for this are many, I believe, but I shall refer to only one or two.
Agriculture is practically the only Canadian industry whose prices are controlled by supply and demand. The price of manufactured goods bears a very close relationship to and is largely governed by the cost of production. Lawyers, doctors and professional men in Canada all have a schedule of fees which they adhere to more or less closely. The salaried man knows at the beginning of the year what his income is going to be. Merchants endeavour, and very successfully, to maintain a constant margin of profit between buying and selling prices. Freight rates, passenger rates, telephone rates and so on are controlled by a government board. Government contracts contain a fair wage clause, and labour has its union scale of wages which is recognized by statute. Recently I read in one of the Toronto papers an item stating that a Toronto barber had been haled before the court and fined because he had charged twenty-five cents for a haircut, which was lower than the union wage scale.
Unquestionably, Mr. Speaker, these systems of price maintenance are here to stay. But notwithstanding these schemes for maintaining prices on every hand, the farmer has little or no control over the prices which he obtains for his products. Agencies must be maintained to collect, to process, to grade and to distribute farm products, and they all take their margin of profit. The spread between farmer-producer prices and consumer prices is gradually widening, but little or no effort has been made by the present government to provide a remedy; in fact, the present government immediately on coming into office took steps to destroy the machinery set up by the former administration to assist agriculture by referring the Natural Products Marketing Act to the privy council for a decision as to its validity.
I want it to be understood that I am not suggesting that prices for farm products should be fixed in Canada in the way that was done

by the present administration when it fixed the price for western, wheat. I do, however, agree heartily with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Bertrand), and again this afternoon by the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario (Mr. McNevin) that since this has been done for the western farmer, similar concessions should have been made to the eastern grain grower and the mixed farmer.
May I point out that in many lines of farm production a very large percentage of the production is consumed in the Dominion of Canada. I have before me a bulletin issued by the bureau of statistics, agricultural branch. It is entitled, "The relationship of exports, imports and apparent consumption of agricultural commodities to Canadian production." I find that it gives the percentage of exports to the amount produced in Canada in the year 1935. for example, and I shall give the house only three or four commodities as an example of what I mean. In 1935, of oats, for instance, we exported only 3-9 per cent of our production; 9-11 per cent of barley; 2-4 per cent of potatoes and 7-9 per cent of cattle. Of our total meats we exported 12 per cent; of our total dairy products, 6-8 per cent; of eggs, -6 per cent; of our total poultry products, -8 per cent. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, it is the price we receive for this small exportable surplus which, in a great many instances, determines the domestic price. Why should the price received for the eight per cent of our cattle exported control the price of cattle in our home market? And yet it undoubtedly does.
In a bulletin which I received from the industrial and development council of Canadian meat packers I find this significant sentence:
It is evident that with a duty of six cents per pound on dressed beef the Canadian packing industry has been eliminated as a competitive factor in United States markets.
This situation makes market prices for Canadian cattle dependent on United States cattle prices. The value of any cattle in Canada (with some possible minor exceptions) will be what they are worth for export alive to United States and any possible export to Britain. This must obtain in every class of cattle of which there is a surplus over domestic requirements.
This is surely a case of the tail wagging the dog. It is a most unsatisfactory and unprofitable method of determining domestic prices. In many instances our Canadian farm products compete in foreign markets with the cheap goods of other nations which have lower wage scales and lower standards of living. The search of the present government for markets in foreign countries, no matter how successful,

The Address-Mr. Kinley
can never solve the problem of the farmers' price structure in Canada. Some leadership must be given, whether we like it or not, towards maintaining a reasonable price structure for farm products in this dominion. Other countries have taken drastic steps in this direction. Australia some time ago put into effect what is known as the Patterson scheme of bonusing exports to help maintain a profitable price level at home. New Zealand two or three years ago set the price of butter fat in that country, where the production of dairy products is the most important industry, and as yet its government has not paid out one cent on that account. Great Britain has established a quota system, in order to maintain farm prices by means of the quantitative regulation of imports. France, Germany and Italy have bonused the production of cereals in their respective countries and have erected impassable trade barriers against these commodities.
The former administration passed the Natural Products Marketing Act, under which some twenty-two schemes were operating when the act was declared ultra vires by the privy council, to which body it had been submitted by the present government for adjudication as to its validity. In contrast to all this, the present government has done little or nothing toward assisting agriculture in Canada to maintain a stable price for farm products. Fluctuations in prices continue with startling rapidity, and the Canadian farmer is powerless to prevent them. If Canadian agriculture is to survive, something must be done and done quickly. I heard a responsible man not so very long ago say that a very large number of our farmers are to-day bankrupt. He placed the proportion at fifty per cent. I am not going to say that such a percentage is at all correct, but I know the number is very large and is gradually increasing. It is little wonder, therefore, that everybody in this country is condemning in no measured terms the inaction of the present government. It is high time that action should be taken, and I suggest to the government that if they are unable to cope with a situation they should make way for somebody else.
For the reasons I have outlined I intend to vote for the amendment which was proposed by my leader. In the words of that amendment:
. . . the government has failed ... to show a proper realization of the serious economic conditions existing in all sections of Canada, as evidenced by . . . widespread distress which prevails in agriculture; and has failed-
Dismally.
-to take appropriate measures to relieve such conditions.
I should like to conclude by quoting one sentence which I read recently in a trade journal and which expresses in a few words my sentiments regarding the great basic industry of agriculture:
It can be said that agriculture is God's chosen profession, and nothing can be nobler than producing foodstuffs for the Canadian people. If the producer cannot get his just reward, then no other class of people can enjoy permanent prosperity. The farmer in the last analysis asks for nothing more than a square deal with a decent standard of living in the farm homes of Canada.
