speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this house we have assembled 245 members, and each one has an intimate knowledge of conditions in some part of Canada. They are men and women who in the aggregate know more about the country and have more accurate information than could be obtained from any other source. This knowledge was exhibited at the outset by the mover (Mr. Matthews) and the seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address. I have a great deal of pleasure in adding my congratulations to those they have already received.
As the debate has continued, some have spoken of our achievements and other have told of our problems and our difficulties. But with it all I am sure we shall all subscribe to the thought that in spite of those difficulties and our problems, we all feel thankful for the many blessings and advantages we enjoy. Canada is a good country. In fact at this time I can think of no other that is superior. We have freedom in this country, and in the midst of a troubled and perplexed world we have a degree of security which is assuring. Our associations with outside peoples are most fortunate, and we believe that in spite of conditions which exist and pending disasters that seem to have threatened us during the last few years we are making economic and social progress.
To judge of our country we must compare it with others; and when we make these comparisons I am certain we shall agree that Canada is in the very forefront of progress. Trade after all is the industrial blood stream of the nation. We are told that we are sixth in foreign trade in the world, that our domestic exports are fourth of all countries of the world, and I am sure we agree that this is a splendid position for a country such as Canada. We are told also by experts, men who admire us from the outside, that Canada is a bright spot in the industrial life of the world and that her immediate future is full of promise.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) thinks we have failed, and he has so expressed
2S6
The Address-Mr. Kinley

it in the amendment which he moved to the address. Well, this is natural. As leader of the opposition he is supposed to criticize and show the imperfections of the government. But I am reminded that he was formerly a member of the Bennett government. Being a member of that government, he has memories; from his speech the other day I think one can draw the conclusion that he thinks he was most severely and wrongfuly criticized in the days that are gone, and now that he is leader of the opposition he is going to return the compliment. He would like a reduction of taxes, but he is not so enthusiastic about the removal of the three per cent excise tax. And when he talks about a reduction- of taxes and enumerates in this chamber the taxes that have been placed on the statute books, we are reminded that most of those taxes were placed there by a former government, and for a purpose, that purpose being to pay the enormous burden caused by the war. That burden is still with us and is still growing. While we thought that during recent years some way would be found to overtake and lessen this burden, we have discovered that we must now spend millions of dollars in order to defend this country and make it safe as a part of the British Empire, and therefore we cannot see, in view of the spending which is imposed upon the government, how this reduction in taxes which he talks about can take place.
The right hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Bennett) led the opposition in this house for three years, and he was most critical; he also thought that the government had failed. He recently decided to move to another land, and in being entertained before he left he took the people of this country into his confidence. He has now decided that the church has failed. Well, I should hate to think that the church has failed, and it would be sad to visualize a country where there is no church. I do not think the church has failed in Canada; but, like all progressive movements, all movements for uplifting the people and raising the standards of the citizenship of the country, the church can never completely accomplish its purpose and in this world it will never reach its goal. On the one hand we have the present leader of the opposition saying that the government has failed; on the other we have the leader who has retired from the field saying that the church has failed in this country. I am sure that we all have faith in this country; but some hon. members, in trying to inform us how the administration fails, will go to distant countries and exhibit to this house what they think is a good picture of prosperity there.

The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. [DOT]Coldwell), who almost always contributes something of interest to the discussions in this house, the other day told us how well New Zealand was getting along. Well, my information is that New Zealand enjoyed a period of artificial prosperity induced by a program of expanding expenditures in public works and in other ways. But they found it too great a strain on their resources, and they are now endeavouring to restore the situation by making drastic restrictions in imports in the hope that this will relieve the financial strain. It looks as if they will be required to pay for their carnival of prodigality.
I have before me a circular that came to our office in the course of business. It deals with New Zealand's import licensing system and advises that a further cablegram has now been received from New Zealand stating:
The New Zealand Finance Minister has decided to admit any goods ordered on or before December 5, 1938, irrespective of the date of shipment of such goods, provided the quantities are not abnormal. As to orders received since December 5, the present status is that the importer in New Zealand must get a licence from his government to import before it is safe for the Canadian exporter to forward shipment.
It seems to me that the story about New Zealand's prosperity can well be taken with a grain of salt. Our friends to the left refer from time to time to Norway and Sweden, which countries they say we should copy. Their example, we are told, is well worth considering. I have never been in Sweden, but in our harbour I have visited vessels from both Norway and Sweden and have talked to their crews. I have seen how their men are fed, and I know that Canadian sailors would not be satisfied with what is given sailors from Sweden and Norway. I know also that these people are undermining the marine trade of this country. Through the low wages they pay their crews they are able to compete successfully against our people. I have seen these vessels come and go for years, and I know that there are members of crews who will desert at every opportunity in order to remain in Canada.
I took the trouble to prepare from the records of the League of Nations a statement of wages paid different classes of men in Norway, Sweden, Great Britain and Canada. The list comprises shipyard workers, machinists, shipwrights, helpers and labourers, carpenters, bricklayers, electricians, cabinet - makers, street-car conductors and motormen, machinists generally, truck drivers, bakers, and civic labourers. I find that in every instance the wages paid in Canada are a great deal more than those paid in Norway and Sweden.

The Address-Mr. Kinley
But, we are told, the social structure in those countries is so good that there are no monopolies in Norway and Sweden. The fact is, however, that the most iniquitous millionaire of the century carried on his work in Sweden through a match monopoly, and his operations had their repercussions in other countries. He finally came to an untimely end by shooting himself.
However, there are difficulties in this country, and as we all know, unemployment is one of them. To-day it is really the fly in the ointment; it is the thing that troubles us most. But why should that be? I wonder if our people are making a really determined and intelligent effort. Some responsibility rests, of course, with the government, and there is some responsibility with those who are unemployed; but I am referring especially to the intelligent, virile and strong people of the country, who, after all, are the people who must make it a success or a failure. On Sunday morning it was my privilege to listen to a missionary from the island of Formosa, which is about as large as the island of Vancouver. I am told there are over five million people there, and one wonders sometimes how they get along. The same is true of many other countries with large populations. But here in Canada we have eleven million people with great resources and a vast territory, and it seems to me that if the matter were seriously considered by every Canadian citizen, a way would be found of providing employment for our people.
I was very much interested yesterday to hear the speech of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). He spoke of the responsibility of private industry. He said that private industry had a responsibility in Canada to see that men were employed, and I agree with him. Perhaps there should be a more extensive system of subsidized apprenticeship in order that every man could learn a trade. When I think of unemployment I think naturally of my own riding. In my counties there are men who naturally wish to work at sea. On the seacoast of Nova Scotia we have the greatest commercial fishing centres of Canada, and I am constantly approached by young men who are anxious to get a berth so as to work on the sea instead of being unemployed.
I have known for a long time that the Canadian mercantile marine and'the marine interests in this country were not very considerate of Canadians. I came across, in the Financial Post, an article that startled- me. May I read it:
Whose Vessels are They?
Should Canada contribute to the support of the British navy? A member of the staff of
the Financial Post recently in London was asked by many English people when Canada intended to carry its "share" of the load of protecting Canadian shipping on the North Atlantic.
This question is one capable of provoking a prolonged discussion in any group. In the ensuing argument there is one factor that is likely to be overlooked. Not a determining point, it is nevertheless important.
The ships on the North Atlantic that carry cargoes between Canada and the United Kingdom are British ships. The Post staff man came home on a C.P.R. ship. It had been built in Britain and was of British registry. It carried a crew of 381, of whom only one was a Canadian. That man was the railway ticket agent!
In the twelve months to March 31, 1937, 911 vessels of British registry carrying cargo entered Canada with 1,523,557 tons of freight from the United Kingdom. The vessels were manned by a crew of 114,211 men. In the same period, one vessel of Canadian registry, carrying cargo, with seventy-five tons of freight and with a crew of thirty-nine, entered Canada from the United Kingdom.
Now we know that the head of the Canadian Pacific Steamships and the Canadian Pacific Railway is interested in youth. He is a public-spirited man who is anxious to see unemployment ended, and it is to his interest to see that it is ended. But how can we do away with unemployment if men of that standing forget that the people of this country must be employed in industry if unemployment is to be ended? I am told that these railway companies are anxious to have more immigration into this country. And I believe that if fifty or one hundred thousand people came into this country from Europe they would be employed within a year or two. But I am more interested in the men of Nova Scotia who in the past sailed to every country in the world and on all the seas. These men desire employment; it is a natural ambition and a legitimate claim that they should have the first openings in the services of this country. They are not looking for big wages. From Vancouver we are told that it is a matter of wages. What our men want is a chance to start to learn something; it is a question not of wages but of getting employment. When the statute of Westminster was passed I thought it was the emancipation of the coasting trade and the merchant marine; but concurrent with the enactment of that statute was also enacted the merchant shipping agreement; which handed back everything we gained as far as shipping is concerned, and Canada's coasting trade to-day-differing from that of the United States and other countries-seems wide open.
With regard to relief, we realize that there has been an abnormal situation in western
The Address-Mr. Kiriley

Canada and that the effects of those years of drought are still being felt. Were it not for that condition, good as our progress has been it would probably have been much better, and the ministry could have presented a better report. In Nova Scotia it is hard to think of a farmer on relief. We very rarely have a failure of crops, and whatever else he has, he at least has enough to eat and is able to keep himself warm. In my riding there is no relief. I have under my hand a report relating to the municipal council of Lunenburg, which appeared the other day. It states:
While other municipal councils in the province are raising their tax rates, Lunenburg's governing body gave assurance in their opening session to-day that the rate for the municipality of Lunenburg would be lowered again this year. For the past three years this county has been favoured by a reduction in rates, and it is expected that the present rate of $3.10 will be brought down to the $3 level.
This condition prevails not only in the municipality of Lunenburg but in the town of Lunenburg, where the tax rate has been reduced and they are retiring bonds; also in the towns of Bridgewater and Liverpool. These are the three important towns in my riding.
Hon. members may wonder how this comes about. The year book shows that we in Nova Scotia earn less than in practically any other province except the other maritime provinces, that we have less per capita wealth, and that our production is less. Still, in my riding there is no direct relief. Thrift is a virtue which I commend to the people of Canada. It seems to me that the municipality is primarily responsible for relief, notwithstanding the contributions from the federal government and the provincial government. But if the municipalities do not realize that this relief is a canker in the life of this country, there is little hope of accomplishing much. It is probably true that in urban districts the position is worse than in the rural districts. That is to be expected because in the artificial life of cities when people are out of work they have no resources with which to maintain themselves.
With regard to unemployment, I think that youth training is the most important matter with which we have to deal. Time will cure the troubles of the older people, but teaching our youth to be good, responsible citizens is the right place to start to solve this problem. If a young man lives to the age of twenty-two or twenty-three loafing around pool-rooms and becoming a drifter, he is not apt to be much of an asset to his country. As a subject for youth training in the maritimes, navigation at once presents itself. I am glad that I succeeded in getting the marine section of the

Department of Transport to open a navigation school in a principal seaport town in my riding. It should be part of the public education from a technical standpoint in Nova Scotia. Every boy who exhibits a desire to go to sea should get training in navigation. Six years ago parliament passed the Canada Shipping Act. Sometimes laws aggravate unemployment. In my riding the Canada Shipping Act aggravated unemployment. Our men were men of experience. They go to sea and become expert sailors by experience. But they did not have certificates. But when this shipping act came into effect they were put out of their jobs; they were told they were not fit because they had not a certificate. I approached the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) and explained the matter; he sent his technical officers to Nova Scotia, got these men together and held examinations, and in the town where I live fifty or sixty of them passed. This year again we had some trouble with certificates; the minister again sent his technical officers to the province, and I believe they found a satisfactory solution of the matter.
With the advent of the internal combustion engine we should be training engineers capable of handling the Diesel engine. This is a new field of endeavour for young people. I believe that the Diesel engine will bring back wooden shipping along the Nova Scotia coast. These wooden ships with Diesel engines are very economical; they do not need a large crew and they have good speed. Quite a number have been built during the last few years; we have had a revival of wooden shipbuilding in Nova Scotia by reason of the Diesel engine. I want our men to be taught to be good engineers to operate these boats.
We sometimes hear about public works, and we are told that public works are not much good to help unemployment. Well, public works are good. Along the coast of Nova Scotia there are many fishermen who hardly earn enough to get by, and if there are public works which enable them to earn $50 or $75, it just makes it possible for them to get along comfortably and helps out the situation splendidly, in addition to providing the breakwaters and wharves that are necessary in order that the fishermen may properly carry on their business. I think public works, as they apply to the sea coast, are absolutely necessary, and the men give a return for the money they receive.
I am glad that the speech from the throne contained a reference to the fishermen. That is a compliment, because it is not often that the fishermen are mentioned there. At page

The Address-Mr. Kinley
27 of Hansard for January 16, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) quoted from the speech from the throne, as follows:
Continuous improvement in the position of the fishing industry as a whole has been reflected-
He stopped there, and said that his reports were to the contrary. As a matter of fact, however, this is what was said in the speech from the throne:
Continuous improvement in the position of the fishing industry as a whole has been reflected in annual increases for the past few years in the aggregate amounts received by the fishermen from their work. The Department of Fisheries have given, and will continue to give, increased attention to the problem of marketing. The government have also assisted fishermen substantially through direct aid.
Well, we are not satisfied with the condition of our fishermen, but we think a great deal has been done. I must remind the house that it was a Liberal government that first appointed a separate Minister of Fisheries in the person of Hon. Cyrus Macmillan; and during the last few years a great deal of attention has been paid to this industry. Loans have been granted, with the cooperation of the provincial government. In some provinces direct contributions were made, but in Nova Scotia it was done by way of loan. A collection service has been established in eastern Nova Scotia, where the worst conditions prevailed, and this year nearly two million pounds of fish have been brought from that section to the market at Halifax. Then I am reminded that the provincial government has been giving a bounty of one dollar per quintal on salted fish, for the export trade. After that had been in existence for two years it was reduced to seventy-five cents, but the fisherman still got his fifty cents while the owners of the vessel got twenty-five cents.
Our hon. friends to the left ask what we have done for the fishermen. I recall when a delegation from my county came to the government, before 1930, complaining that conditions in the export trade were bad and asking for a bounty of fifty cents in connection with salted fish. That request was refused. Then, when the Liberals came into power in Nova Scotia, with the cooperation of this government a bounty of a dollar was paid the fishermen in order that they might have a fair show in the export trade in competition with other countries doing the same thing. There was also a bounty established on seals, which were destroying the fish and causing a great deal of damage. In my riding also, I am proud to say, we have the Nova Scotia fisheries exhibition each year, which 71492-19
was honoured last year by the attendance of the Minister of Transport. That exhibition has been subsidized since its inception, and we feel that it is a great advertisement for the fisheries of this country. That subsidy is also something we obtained from the Liberal government.
I should like to refer to old age pensions. As hon. members know, the old fisherman was always a problem on the coast of Nova Scotia. He might possess considerable wealth one day; then along came a storm and his nets would be swept away. We find that as the fishermen get older most of them have very little of this world's goods, so the old age pension did a great deal for the fishermen of Nova Scotia, making an asset of many an old man who had been a liability to his sons, and bringing some social justice to these people along our shores.
When we came here in 1935 we had high hopes in regard to the trade treaty. I must confess that I was a little disappointed, when the trade treaty was consummated, that fish of the cod family were not included in it. But we thought perhaps there would be a chance in the future. Some fish, swordfish, halibut and so on, were covered by the treaty, and the production of those fish immediately increased. In my riding we have the largest fishing fleet in Canada, and I thought if we could get a trade treaty with the United States, giving us entry to the best market in the world for fresh cod, halibut and other Canadian fish, we would be doing something for the people whom we try to represent. Now this three-way trade agreement between Great Britain, the United States and Canada has been consummated, bringing with it reductions in the duties on fish entering the United States. I believe that will do more to stabilize and assist our fishing industry than anything that has been done by this parliament for many years.
In 1932 we had an imperial trade conference in Ottawa. Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin delivered an address in this very chamber, and speaking of empire trade he said that there were two ways in which increased preferences could be given, either by lowering tariffs among ourselves or by raising them against others. Then he said:
The choice between those two must be governed largely by local considerations, but subject to that it seems to us that we should endeavour to follow the first rather than the second course.
He was in favour of the lowering of duties. I think this trade treaty, though it is to extend for three years, will be more stable than the treaty of 1935 because it is linked up with the British trade agreement, and the

The Address-Mr. Kinley

British agreement with the United States is of greater importance in the industrial life of the world. Of course if the British trade agreement fails, we shall get back some of the things which our friends say we lost but which probably were given so that the cod. fish of the maritimes might get into the United States market.
Let me say I was very proud of the position taken in Nova Scotia by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) just after the treaty was signed. He represents a great apple growing constituency, one enjoying a preference in a free market. On the other hand fishermen have had to enter a market carrying a high duty, a market which was by no means a free one. I might add that apple growing is also carried on to a considerable extent in the constituency I have the honour to represent, which adjoins that of the minister. I believe the minister spoke for the people in Nova Scotia when he said that, after all, apples still have a good preference, and will continue to supply the British market.
I do not believe trade is divine in its origin, but I am of the opinion that the Divine Architect of the Universe had some regard for trade when the world was created. We find oranges and bananas' growing in warm countries, fish in the cold waters of the Atlantic, minerals in the unexplored regions of the frozen north. All this is a challenge to man. Trade is a challenge to man to be industrious and to be diligent in his business operations. After all, trade is the life of the nation. Has any hon. member entered a town and heard someone say, "Oh what a dead town!" What did that person mean? He meant there was no trade-nothing moving. No one knows better than the leader of the opposition that if a man's blood stops circulating, he is dead. If water remains quiet, it becomes stagnant, and develops power only when it begins to move and when there is circulation. The same reasoning applies to the trade of a country. The circulation of trade is what makes the people prosperous. It is my belief that Canada's exceptionally good position as a trading country means that our future is assured and that the government in office deserves credit for this achievement. '
The West Indies treaty has been the cause of much discussion, and the hope shared by hon. members from the maritime provinces is that we may obtain a better deal under that treaty. Criticism has been lodged in the country about a lack of notice at an earlier date. Hon. members can well see that in view of consideration of the three-way British-
[Mr. Kinloy.l
Canada-United States trade agreement it would not have been a good idea to have given earlier notice and thereby cause embarrassment in connection with the arrangemnts with Great Britain and the United States. Notice to the West Indies was given immediately after the trade arrangements with the United States and Great Britain were signed, and I believe in due time hon. members from the maritimes will find the amended trade treaty will be signed, will exhibit their desires, and will show that we represent our people in an intelligent manner.
I have spoken about the low earnings per capita of the people of Nova Scotia, and have pointed out that no direct relief has been paid in Queens-Lunenburg. From those observations hon. members may have received the impression that we have little culture, that we do not look after our social services, and that we are lacking in intelligence. I would remind hon. members that such is far from the case. I have felt grateful to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which has given us an opportunity to give expression to the cultural side of our people. The broadcasts over the Canadian network of the concerts of the Lunenburg glee club have left no doubt as to the cultural development in that part of the country. We are of the opinion, too, that the contest in which the Bluenose took part was well handled by the broadcasting corporation. Both the race and the musical activities are expressions of the cultural development in Queens-Lunenburg, the riding I have the honour to represent.
In closing, let me point out that the price spreads committee of which the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) was chairman, stated that the fishermen of Canada needed markets, and that there was no trouble about production. As a matter of fact, we have over-production, but we need more markets. In Canada, while we consume only twenty-six pounds of fish per capita a year, we produce one hundred and twenty pounds per capita. Hon. members will see that there is a large surplus which must go somewhere, and it will be recognized at once that trade treaties for the fishermen of the Atlantic coast are of paramount importance. We must have such treaties if those men are to live and prosper, and I hope the fishermen will get a larger share of the consumer's dollar.
We hear fears expressed to the effect that democracy is imperilled. Democracy is not easily attained; it is militant and demands a virile, industrious and alert people. I do not believe the peoples of Europe want dictatorships, but they have sunk below the level of men who can govern themselves. The

The Address-Mr. Hayhurst
question occurs to me: How long in this country can men who cannot support themselves govern themselves? The question arises as to whether or not we should take a firmer stand and the captains of industry, the governments and the alert people of the country join together in an effort to eradicate unemployment which, after all, is the real and serious problem which faces us.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I quote the last sentence of the speech from the throne:
In this critical time of the world's affairs, I pray that Divine Providence may guide and bless your deliberations.
Yes, "guide and bless your deliberations." At the present time the international situation calls for enlightened leadership. Canada is placed in a position where it may give leadership to	the nations.	Surely by	ourexertions we might do something to save ourselves and	by our example	might	dosomething to	save others.	The	health	and
happiness of mankind are of more importance than the piling up of armaments, something which is most distasteful. Out of the anguish and distress of to-day it seems to me that it would be possible to make Canada one of the leading nations of the world.
The public	ravings of	some	people	in
various countries are creating an attitude of fear not only among neighbouring peoples but among ourselves. The powers of fear and hate have superseded the power of reason. The defenders of democracy are being challenged, and that implies the possibility of conflict. May Providence guide us from such conflict, which can lead only to chaos. Public opinion in neutral countries would and could change for good the balance of our civilization.
Democracy as practised by this government is said to be aimless, inefficient and eco-nomicalb' unjust. It is time the government did some really democratic planning. Democracy in Canada does not give freedom or opportunity to the mass of the people on account of economic inequalities. I ask, what good is freedom to a starving man? He cannot eat or drink freedom. The situation is critical. Time is a vital factor. The world is changing rapidly, and dilatoriness can easily give the fascist dictatorships the control they desire. The road to victory lies in taking the offensive, and the first offensive should be the crystallization of public opinion against inroads on our liberties. We must be quick to organize against such inroads while there is still time. We cannot be silent in the face of injustice; for liberty must arouse respect in the minds of our people. Those who know 71492-19}
what liberty means will not surrender. Democracy should adopt a counter-strategy to fascism, but this strategy must have aims which are worth working for. It has been said that democracy stands for liberty, equality and happiness. We should not be afraid to advertise these facts to the world.
The armies of unemployed in the world, the economic interdependence brought about by booms and slumps, take from us the power of judgment. It is impossible for us to penetrate beneath the mask which our enemies prepare, and thus has been killed the very idea of freedom. At times it seems that mankind is again heading into a new dark age. The search seems to be for power. Witness Japan in her lust for imperial dominion, carrying on a ruthless warfare with China. Angry passions rule nations. Making war in order to gain economic objectives has become the adopted policy of many nations.
Security is all that people want, but insecurity has made people careless; for we are not free if we are helpless to keep our security. The policy of to-day is such that foreign glory has been presented as a substitute for a higher standard of living. Social reform must await the completion of arms programs. The normal habits of freedom will be difficult to attain in lands where dictatorships have flourished. Hate and passion have taken the place of free debate, and who knows whether it will not end in revolution or international conflict? The urge for freedom should be powerful enough to make us organize and be prepared for eventualities.
Democracy will survive only if its most ardent devotees prefer it to other ideologies. Democracy has a reai responsibility. It must oppose the encroachment of dictatorships, or the struggles of our fathers will prove to have been in vain. We should not compromise on fundamental principles. It seems that we must choose between an open-door economy and a closed economy, between open diplomacy and secret diplomacy, and if we choose the former we must realize that it must be based upon faith in each other's pledges. Too often these pledges have been broken. We have compromised on armaments only to find that other nations have not kept their agreements.
With purpose and decision we should plan for a better society. No doubt our society should eliminate poverty and unemployment, and it is within our power to do so. Can we remove these evils; can we hand on the freedom won to the generations that are yet to come?
The Address-Mr. Hay hurst

I shall never forget the time of the recent crisis in London. One day I listened at Hyde Park corner to the speeches of various people. I was particularly interested in the startling remarks of a tall, gaunt, hollow-eyed man who was denouncing Mr. Chamberlain. He said that Mr. Chamberlain had gone to see the barbarian in the barbarian mountains, and that he might have brought back peace, but it was peace with dishonour. It is not for me to pass judgment upon him. Later I visited Westminster, with all its history. Here is the very cradle of our parliamentary institutions. Here the lives of the great men remind us that the administration of the empire or of any part of it has been far from perfect. But where do you find perfection in democratic government, which believes in a maximum of liberty for the individual? This very liberty gives us freedom to do so many things that we are bound to make mistakes somewhere. The administration of the empire, I repeat, is far from perfect. There are many stains on our record -stains on the record of our treatment of the native peoples of Africa-stains on the record of the treatment of our Indians-but these stains are abhorrent to us and we are anxious to wipe them out. We stand for justice, mercy and beneficence. Far from perfect, the record of our parliamentary history will compare favourably with the history of any other people with a different form of government.
It is difficult to find a satisfactory basis of classification of the governments of the world, but in any such classification the parliamentary form of government, imperfect though it be, is still our greatest heritage. Conditions will not remain as they are. We shall have changes. Indeed to-day the great need is to change. We have witnessed the adoption of the federal system of government in Canada and Australia, and have seen the unification of South Africa. The process will not stop there. Science and geography will make us change as the needs arise. Our achievements in the past will urge us on to greater and better liberties, and we shall ease and lift the burdens now borne by many. Every type of civilization, every cause, however hopeless, has always found defenders who would accept martyrdom in its behalf.
In this connection I wish to read a passage from The Things Men Fight For, by H. H. Powers:
But while our preference is not due to the superiority of our civilization, the superiority of our civilization is largely due to our preference. The most ideal civilization would die if its devotees did not passionately prefer it, just as the most perfect species of animal

would perish if it did not cherish and protect its young with unreasoning devotion. Hence our unreasonable preferences as measured by the inherent quality of things, are justified as the only thing that can gi' e our way of life a fighting chance in the great struggle for survival.
It is invidious to make comparisons, and I do not propose to do so. I shall simply say that our ideals are the result of a long and arduous struggle. The yoke on our shoulders has been lightened by the struggles of the past, and now we must hold fast to the intangible things that have made our empire great.
The nations of the world are engaged in a mutual effort to strangle each other by war, by raising tariffs, or by lowering quotas. Every nation is trying to increase its exports but is unwilling to import. The imports of one nation are, however, the exports of another, so that in so far as world imports are reduced world exports are thereby correspondingly reduced. Until, therefore, nations generally are prepared to increase their imports, world imports cannot increase.
The reason for dwindling world trade will accordingly be found when it is discovered why nations wish to reduce imports. The individual merchant is vitally interested to see the removal of the obstacles which each nation places in the way of imports, and a consequent expansion in total world trade. He is personally concerned in the discovery and removal of those causes which have led nations to attempt to restrict imports by means of tariffs, quotas, and exchange restrictions.
The dragon's teeth of discord are being sown in countries of eastern Europe. Will this break down our civilization? Will bitter propaganda kill all originality of mind and creative thought? Will democracy survive? If it will, it must be reinforced. The dark clouds of war are casting their shadows over the world to-day. Italy has struck, Japan has struck, and Spain is experiencing the horrors of internecine strife. It is a grim outlook. Different ideologies are attempting to win converts by brute force. Fascism is the dominant force in many lands. We know that the violent words of Herr Hitler were supported by' a tremendous increase in armaments in Germany. It seemed to anyone in London on that memorable day when the German chancellor delivered his speech that the question was one either of war or of peace. It would not have mattered greatly who had represented the British; he would have had to consider this cold and unpleasant reality- to be or not to be? That was the question. It would be presumptuous on my part to pass judgment on what happened at Munich. I

The Address-Mr. Hay hurst
was in England at the time, and there was both praise and criticism of the Munich pact. The dramatic events which succeeded each other in quick succession are now history. The consequence of the decisions reached by Chamberlain, Bonnet, Hitler and Mussolini will have tremendous results in the destiny of Europe. Our international relations seem to be confused. Our conscience is shocked by reports in newspapers from day to day. The Spanish situation makes us wonder how it will all end. Statements in the press, on the radio or in reviews perplex and confuse us; so we may well pray for guidance in our deliberations.
Has Munich merely postponed the evil day for a day more terrible? What a terrible state of affairs! Look at China; here is the Daily Telegraph's Supplement of June 27, 1938, on China. What does it say?
Ruin and terror in China!
Bombing has maimed and killed thousands, destroying homes and industries.
Burning has wiped out towns, villages, crops and stocks.
Floods have engulfed immense areas of fertile land.
Famine is transforming China's peaceful folk into wandering terror-stricken refugees.
The same applies to Spain. Public indignation in a democracy changes the course of events, sometimes for the worse. It is possible that the public indignation which caused the resignation of Sir Samuel Hoare at the time of the Hoare-Laval plan was primarily responsible for Italy joining Germany.
Timidity and lack of knowledge and foresight have done much in the past few years to allow a handful of men to paralyze whole nations, but we must not despair. We must learn to draw from misfortune the means of future strength. It is the hour, not for despair but for courage, remembering that justice is as important as peace.
The greatest wastage in Canada to-day is the wastage of our youth. The government should give a lead in defining democracy; should tell us plainly what the benefits of democracy are, and should help our young people by means of scholarships or in other ways to become leaders. Democracy can survive only if men and women know what it means. Democracy should work so that our young people will be enthusiastic in its cause.
Regarding the subject of democracy I will take a quotation from Constructive Democracy. Here is a piece by the Marquess of Lothian:
But the weakness of liberal democracy has been-
And this applies also to Canadian Liberalism. -that it has not hitherto been able to establish economic liberty or equality. It gives liberty
to those who can command property or credit to initiate and conduct economic enterprise. But it does not yet give liberty to the man without capital. It is not liberty to be free to look for a job when there is no job to be found. And it is not equality to have access to the multitudinous goods which capitalism puts in the shop window when, through no fault of your own, you have no money in your pocket with which to buy them.
And what of the new Canadians in our land? Our ancestors came from nearly every European country. We have in Canada over 600.000 citizens of Ukranian descent, and they are asking us to take an interest in them. During the past twenty years the Ukrainians have been struggling to establish once more in the Ukraine a motherland which could be called their own. They enjoy democracy and would uphold it in this country. It seems to be the dream of every Ukrainian that they have in Europe a free Ukraine as their motherland. In general they have remained a democratic nation and continue to believe in the liberties of democracy.
I have received several communications from friends of the Ukrainian people, and they are desirous that an impartial Ukrainian viewpoint concerning Ukrainian problems in Europe be given. I have before me a declaration from Ukrainian Canadians and friends regarding the Ukraine. In publishing this declaration the committee hopes, first: to stop false representations of the Ukrainian cause to international opinion as sponsored by some foreign influences, and, second, to provide true information to the British authorities and thus enable the British Empire to take part in a settlement of the Ukrainian question on behalf of her citizens in Canada. This is the declaration of Ukrainian Canadians and friends regarding the Ukraine:
The grave danger to world peace during the European crisis which resulted from internal minority problems in Czechoslovakia, has shown clearly to the powers of Europe, as well as to the rest of the world, that minority problems within the artificial boundaries of post-war European states composed of several nationalities are dangerous sources of strife and are productive of great international conflicts. At this moment, we, the British citizens of Ukrainian origin, enjoying the privileges of free government, feel that it is our supreme duty to raise our voice in the interests of world peace, the British Empire, and a just and permanent solution of the Ukrainian problem. That problem involves the largest subjugated nationality in Europe of to-day. We are supported also by Canadian citizens who, though not of Ukrainian nationality, are friends of Ukrainian liberation.
The Ukrainian problem concerns the vital interests of over forty millions of Ukrainian people, a number equal to the population of France or Italy, who inhabit a solid area of more than one million square kilometers between the Carpathian and the Caucasus mountains in a great arc north of the Black sea.
The Address

Mr. Hayhurst

This entire territory and its people with state traditions dating from 862 A.D. were again united into one sovereign Ukrainian state by the act of January 22nd, 1919, on the basis of the Wilsonian principle of selfdetermination.
Blockaded and attacked from the north by soviet red armies, from the east by the monarchist Russian armies of Generals Denikin and Wrangel, from the west by Poland, and from the south by the armies of Roumania, this newly created power in eastern Europe for three years without support from the great allied powers heroically endeavoured to defend its borders from these enemies and at the same time to check the waves of Russian communism threatening western Europe. However, under the weight of simultaneous and successive blow's of overwhelmingly greater armies, and burdened with the outbreak of a deadly typhoid epidemic, Ukraine finally collapsed before it was able to exert its stabilizing effect upon post-war Europe. This rich Ukrainian state, so important economically and strategically, w'as nevertheless partitioned, its people degraded to the level of "minorities" and divided between the nationally-mixed powers, Czechoslovakia, Roumania, Poland and the Soviet Union. By incorporating considerable parts of the Ukrainian territory and population within their political boundaries, all these states from the very beginning of their existence after the great war and the Russian revolution, became the breeding grounds of dangerous national struggles, oppressions, hatreds and fears, as well as potential sources of a new world war.
During the past twenty years the Ukrainian people, under the four occupant powers have experienced various degrees of cultural, religious, economic and particularly political oppression, including mass pacifications, and famine policies. Not the least of the grievances was the fact that this great nation v'as deprived, through censorship, suppression, and terrorism, of an opportunity to speak freely of its cause in the international forum.
It is for this reason that we, the citizens of Ukrainian origin in the free British Empire, together with the friends of the Ukrainian people in Canada, are moved on behalf of the Ukrainian nation in Europe, to draw to the attention of the British government and other world pov'ers the following points concerning the Ukrainian problem:
1.	In the interest of the balance of power and of a lasting peace in Europe the creation of the Ukrainian sovereign state in the spirit of the acts of January 22nd, 1919, embracing all ethnographically Ukrainian territories, is a historic necessity of wide international significance.
2.	The Ukrainian territories now within the political boundaries of Czechoslovakia, Roumania, Poland and the Soviet Union, must be regarded and dealt with, not as separate minority problems in each case, but as integral parts of the Ukrainian cause as a whole.
3.	To avoid further complications similar to that of the recent European crisis arising from the minority problems of Ceehoslovakia, we strongly urge and earnestly request the great powers, signatories of the Munich pact, to appoint without delay an international commission for the final settlement of the Ukrainian problem in Europe.

Mr. Speaker, we are a country of many races. His Excellency the Governor General in a speech at Halifax said:
The strongest peoples have always been a mingling of races .	.	. but they are only
strong if that mingling is conducted in the proper way. And that proper way is that each accepts and appreciates the qualities of the other.
I shall close my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by quoting a few lines from Shakespeare's King Lear:
If that the heavens do not their visible spirits
Send quickly down to tame these vile offences.
It will come,
Humanity must perforce prey on itself,
Like monsters of the deep.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset, I wish to tender my congratulations to the hon. member who has moved and to the hon. member who has seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I can add nothing to the praise given to them for the manner in which they have fulfilled their task, for no word of mine would add anything to their merit.
During the few years which have elapsed since I was returned as a federal member, it has been my wish that some day, in order that we might enjoy all the better the wonderful speeches delivered in this house, the government, on the recommendation of Mr. Speaker, would provide loud speakers, which would allow those who, like myself, occupy seats in the far corners of the house, to hear better, and to take a more comprehensive view of, the statements of national import made by our legislators. I shall bring up the matter again later on and insist upon it until we succeed in securing that improvement which may seem more or less necessary, but the importance of which is unquestionable.
It is a pleasure for me, Mr. Speaker, to see you presiding again over the debates of this house. The sound judgment which marks your rulings is a great comfort to those who take part in the discussions. May you long remain in the position you occupy; your presence ensures the smooth working of the parliamentary machinery.
I would be remiss in my duty, and my electors, both men and women, would upbraid me if I did not thank publicly the leader of this government (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the sympathy he extended to my constituency on the occasion of the unprecedented disaster which occurred during the night of August 31 to September 1 of last year and which caused such great hardships. The torrential rain which had swollen the Portneuf

The Address-Mr. Gauthier
river had scarcely stopped when we learned that eight human lives had been lost within a radius of about one mile. Two Canadian Pacific Railway employees trapped inside their engine, a mother with her five children swept away by the river which had become a raging torrent; bridges wrecked as if they had been so many toys; dwellings engulfed and carried away like houses of cards, such was the havoc wrought during a single night in the parish of Portneuf. In spite of his heavy duties, the Prime Minister sent us his sympathies that very same night. The people were greatly moved by this splendid gesture of his, and sufferers seemed to regain their spirit.
The government, through the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), who came quite unobtrusively to survey the extent of the losses, extended its help to the stricken municipality.	_
The necessary work is now practically completed and the thanks which I am now extending to the government are well deserved. The action of the Minister of Public Works was very much appreciated by the people. To him also I tender my heartfelt thanks.
I also wish to thank the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) _ for the deep sympathy he has shown, upon his return from Europe, to the sorely tried population of my constituency.
The forthcoming visit of their British majesties to Canada has been, for the last few months, the main topic in the press and among the public men and the whole population of the country. Naturally, our interest is awakened and our curiosity aroused when we realize that the rulers who will be welcomed in this country are the king and queen of Canada, visiting for the first time one of the countries freely associated in the British commonwealth of nations. This democratic gesture does great credit to their majesties; and following the visit of the President of the United States, it is of exceptional significance for the great democracies, and in view of the recent renewal of trade relations, it augurs well for a much more reassuring future and for the realization of a victorious union in the struggle for supremacy between the different nations of the world.
When, from aboard ship, their majesties shall cast their eyes on the Canadian shores, they shall still see the British ensign flying on ships masts and on the house tops the colours of Britain and France as well as those of the head of the Catholic church in the world. However, during their stay in Canada, they will live among a people without a flag. And yet we are a proud people 1 More than ever,
we realize our national responsibilities, we have confidence in our vast resources which, properly used, are such as to make our country entitled to a voice among the nations. However, we Canadians are still without a truly distinctive Canadian flag. I doubt if within the next few weeks to elapse before the arrival of their majesties, we shall have time to reach unanimity of opinion on this matter, in order that we might unfurl a flag which will announce from afar that one is nearing Canada, a truly independent and free nation. We have a long way to go before we are taken seriously and our statements are acknowledged. A flag is only a piece of cloth for the materially minded, but recalls the history of a nation for those who realize all that it stands for.
Although the speech from the throne was severely criticized by some hon. members who saw nothing in it, it contains, however, some very interesting and highly important statements, for instance the government recognizes the necessity of increasing the expenditures for national defence, in view of the world conditions, as well as the need of giving increased attention to the unemployment problem of the country. The assistance given to the youth of the country, worried over the future, shows that the government is determined not to neglect an issue of such importance to our young country. I am greatly concerned by that very consideration which I view from a particular standpoint.
The duty of the government is primarily to provide for those who were born in this country and for those also who, foreign-born, have chosen this country as their land of adoption. Let us hope each and every one of the latter group shall always place the Canadian point of view before any other, and that both these groups of Canadian citizens, in a close and durable unity of purpose, shall help public authorities to improve the economic conditions. Such as have cast a longing look upon our country as the promised land for those who suffer persecution elsewhere, must understand that notwithstanding our spontaneous disapproval of methods which an exaggerated nationalism has inspired, and our deep sympathy for their cause, at the same time, if some of our people can successfully take care of themselves, others must depend on state assistance until better days.
The youth of this country cannot and must not accept any immigration policy tending only, in final analysis, to aggravate their own difficulties. It is not to be wondered at if they have taken the lead in an important movement which can no longer be ignored, which has been rapidly gaining momentum and
The Address-Mr. Gauthier

promises to last indefinitely should we fail to meet their demands. The statement made by the Secretary of State in Montreal last Friday has caused great rejoicing among the younger people. With your permission, Mr Speaker, I shall quote an article published in Le Canada on January 23rd:
Hon. Mr. Rinfret and Immigration. Commonsense has inspired the federal government's decision not to loosen the restrictions on immigration from Europe. Moreover, it is in accordance with public opinion in the whole country. Hon. Mr. Rinfret, Secretary of State, in the speech which he recently made in Montreal, very ably described the situation in which we find ourselves at the moment.
The minister states:
While we deeply deplore the fate of foreign refugees, particularly of those coming from Germany, our sympathy remains with the people of Canada. We are aware that many of our people are unemployed and that certain elements are not easily assimilated to the French and English population of Canada. And the dominion government has come to the decision, while sympathizing with the foreigners, that the existing statutory restrictions on immigration should be maintained. The dominion has no intention of curtailing present restrictions, so long at least as we still have to cope with unemployment in this country.
The editor of Le Canada goes on:
No doubt the systematic persecution endured by the Jewish race in Germany and Austria is bound to move us to pity, but precisely, the dominion government does not want this problem to grow into a question of sentiment. Both wisdom and properly understood charity require the government to look first after the well-being of our Canadian population.
The attitude of the government -would undoubtedly be altogether different if they could get the assurance that all those who desire to enter Canada could settle on the land and earn a living, but such is not the case. In his remarkable book, Canadian Mosaic, Mr. John Murray Gibbon has noted that the flow of Jewish immigration which made its way to Canada around the year 1880 headed chiefly for Montreal and Toronto where they built up the garment industry. The same thing would happen again to-day and we know that neither of these two cities, affected as they are by unemployment, are prepared to receive additional workmen.
According to the census of 1931, out of 156,000 Hebrews settled in Canada, 794 only were farmers. The greater number were employed in the textile industry.
I endorse the views voiced in this editorial and, on behalf of the youth of my province,
I wish to thank the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) for having dispelled the uncertainty which had been brought into their mind by certain newspapers striving too eagerly for the success of a political party on which they are founding their hopes. I have already stated that I wanted no race in particular to be ostracized. Each one is 
entitled to a living in this Canada of ours; on the other hand, all nations have the right to choose their new citizens, even if radio addresses are broadcast from overseas, even if committees are being set up in our country in order to prove that Canada, in the words of Dr. Wallace, principal of Queen's university, in Kingston:
A free and broadminded country, a country that needs more population, has the privilege to show in a practical way that it thoroughly understands the needs of a suffering people. We must not neglect this opportunity.
Had the distinguished doctor lived a century ago he would not have to join such a movement to know whether Canadians can understand the needs of a suffering people; he would realize that sufferings of others need not be added to our own difficulties.
People ostracized by Germany will have the sympathy of all. We have in our midst hundreds of thousands of citizens of Jewish origin. Would it be in their own interest and would it be practical for them to add to that present considerable number thousands of their brothers? We all agree that agriculture has no inducements for them. And is there one Canadian citizen who could reasonably believe that the greatest need in Canada is not more man-power on the farms?
Before accepting further immigration, whichever it may be, let us lead our own people towards lands which would be productive, but for the lack of settlers. The youth training plan is an excellent idea; it should be multiplied fivefold and constitute the chief concern of our governments. The problem of our youth is far more important than any other now before us. Should we fail to solve it we shall have to resign ourselves either to perish economically or to await the leadership of others more bold and concerned with the famous equal distribution of citizens owing the same allegiance in the different colonies which they inhabit.
Our young people must not be let down. They are ever ready to follow whomever will undertake to lead them out of their distressful state. This government has made a good start. Let them continue in spite of all criticism; the people will be grateful to them.
A second interesting point in the speech from the throne is the government's declared intention actively to pursue the execution of its national defence program. I have already expressed my opinion on this question, saying among other things this: A country of 10,000,000 people stimulated by the fever of war, by enthusiasm for the empire, can raise in a few months a considerable army. Public men categorically opposed to participation in

The Address-Mr. Walsh
foreign wars did vote for the sending of troops to the empire's assistance. Circumstances and events proved stronger than men's wills and Canada did take part in a foreign war.
My opinion has not changed. It has not changed, because the circumstances and events to which I was referring will occur again.
We all know about those press campaigns carefully carried out all over the country, those series of speeches having an effect similar to that of the drop of water regularly falling upon the rock, those manoeuvres conducted in different parts of the country with the certitude that politicians, whose election was brought about by the display of posters showing the piled up corpses from wrecked battleships upon a rocky shore will afterwards take refuge among people known as rabid supporters of participation in all the wars of the empire. Such a campaign as we all know, gradually brings the people to such a frame of mind that they finally accept as a necessity something of which they nevertheless disapprove; all such concerted action will bring about a repetition of events which the true dictator, gold, multiplies seemingly as it likes, and it leads to circumstances which men fail to understand and to which they fall easy preys.
No one entertains any doubt about the necessity of national defence; not even he who now has the floor. To my knowledge, no hon. member from this side of the house questions the sincerity of the clear cut statements made by the leader of the government and his ministers, concerning participation in foreign wars. Those who look at things from a Canadian standpoint only- and it is the one which must be considered- are delighted with his firm stand, frankly and admirably Canadian. That stand will, I believe, be the objective of a campaign, already under way, and not unlike the one .waged from 1910 to 1914. There seems to be in Canada, a keener and more deeply rooted public opinion. I heartily wish that such may be the case, for it will then be a harder task, to-morrow, to oust the successor to the Canadian we lost in 1919. Democracy in danger; the empire in danger-for certain sections of the country; the frustrated rights of the provinces-for some other sections; the revamped nationalist doctrine; everything will be used to discredit the man 'who places Canadian patriotism above everything else.
First, he must be dismissed from the scene, and then we shall witness the repetition of what occurred in 1911, 1914 and 1917. I had that picture in mind when the military esti-71492-20	.
mates were first discussed, and it is now even more vivid and enlarged. When the armaments mongers, having disposed of their abominable wares through a war, shall feel like taking a rest, a new crisis will engulf the whole world and Canada, in common with the other countries, will suffer from the flood of unemployed workers from the war industries thrown back into the ranks of those who will not have been able to find employment elsewhere, and the whole game will start all over again.
The whole world is arming, one might say. Unfortunately, such is the excuse offered by those who live from the blood shed during war times and that excuse has found an echo in many quarters.
I have declined, and still decline to be a party to such a farce meant to draw one's attention away from the world wide tragedy. I prefer to devote myself to other activities and to spend my life in bettering the economic life of my country. I stand for Canada above all, for Canada alone, and for Canada forever.

speechtext:
If I had been placed on a
platform in my constituency I would not hesitate to reply in as good French as I could command to many of the arguments of my good friend the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier).
I should like with other hon. members to offer my sincere congratulations to the mover (Mr. Matthews) and the seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address, and particularly to the seconder, who spoke so easily in both French and English, and set an example for every Canadian citizen. I should like, too, to extend my congratulations to the new members of the house. Naturally I regret the reason which brought them here, but I am pleased to see that those who have left us apparently have been replaced to good advantage. I hope the new members will soon fit into the atmosphere of the House of Commons and will discharge their duties to the advantage of their constituencies, and to the country in general.

The Address-Mr. Walsh

May I take this opportunity to extend my congratulations to the hon. members who have recently been elevated to the rank of privy councillors. It is gratifying to sit in the house and see one or another of those with whom one has been associating in the ordinary walks of life selected by their political leader for preferment and advancement within their own party. If one may judge from the names and constituencies, it would seem that the Macs have something which some of the rest of us have not, and that a constituency with the suffix "west" may win the favour of a considerable number of people. Entering the house this afternoon I noticed a floral display on the desk of the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Tomlinson). In passing may I congratulate him upon having attained another milestone in life, and may I wish him much joy and happiness as he goes from one milestone to another.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, may I digress briefly. During the course of the last session there was a somewhat heated debate on a subject centring around the city of Kingston. During the course of that debate I was interrupted by the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario (Mr. Fraser), and in a rather heated reply I used words which might very well be construed as casting a reflection upon his character and reputation. I went to him personally and apologized, and have awaited an opportunity to do so publicly. This is the first opportunity, and may I say here and now that any unworthy ideas or suggestions which could be woven into those words were not intended to be there. I hold the hon. member for Northumberland in the highest esteem and regard, and I believe I do so in common with every hon. member of the house.
It is noticeable that times and conditions of Canada are not good. When times were good and conditions seemed to be improving there was no one on the government side unwilling to take the credit for such improvement. We heard of it in 1937; we heard in 1938 how conditions were improving-and, of course, we were told that conditions were improving only and solely because there was a Liberal government in power in Ottawa. But conditions are not so good to-day. That fact is recognized in the utterances of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and all other hon. members who have taken part in the debate. If the government wishes to take credit in the good years it must of necessity take discredit in the lean years, and must not be 
content to refer to world conditions and suggest that they, as a government, have no responsibility for conditions prevailing in Canada to-day.
If we examine the records of our exports and imports, my reference will be apparent. In 1936 exports were valued at $1,015,000,000; in 1937, $1,110,000,000, and in 1938, $913,000,000, a considerable drop. They still continue to drop, and I have no doubt the report in March, 1939, will not be pleasing to the citizens of Canada. Imports have shown a like tendency. I shall not quote the figures; they speak for themselves and they are already on record. I have noted, too, that revenue returns showed a marked increase in 1936, again in 1937 and again in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1938. If we examine the figures for the year which will end on March 31, 1939, we shall notice that, to the disadvantage of hon. members on the treasury benches, revenues are showing a decided drop. May I point out in passing that this drop is not noticeable, so far as direct taxation on business and industry is concerned. That branch of taxation shows a revenue increase of $20,000,000 to the government. These figures serve to show that despite times which are not good, $20,000,000 more than in previous years has been extracted from business and industry, and it means too, that there is left in business that much less money with which to keep the wheels of industry turning. A government should endeavour to leave in business and industry as much money as possible, because it is that money which keeps industry busy and people employed. But apparently it is the ambition of this government to extract from all sources as much revenue as possible in order to have more money to spend.
I also draw attention to the construction figures for Canada, in order to emphasize the conditions which prevail in this country; and seeing that we were forced to agree last year that conditions were good, and the government claimed credit for that, this year, when conditions are bad, it is only fair to impute the blame to the government. As a further proof of our business recession during the past year I quote the 1937 construction figures, which stood at $304,000,000; in 1938 that figure had dropped to $274,000,000. I call the attention of the house to the paragraph in the speech from the throne in 1938, in which the government says:
It is gratifying to note that, during the past year, there has been a further substantial advance in Canada's economic recovery. Revenues have reached new levels. Trade with other countries has materially expanded.

The Address-Mr. Walsh
There is no such reference in the speech from the throne this year. It is noticeable by its absence; it is absent because times and conditions are not good, and therefore they could not be referred to in the glowing terms which this government liked to use with reference to what had taken place previously, and for which they endeavoured in the past to take credit.
It seems to me that every time there is a discussion of a United States trade agreement it is a bad omen for this country. Conditions in Canada immediately begin to get worse, as we shall notice if we study the trade figures. The benefits that we derived from the empire trade agreements of 1932 have often been emphasized in this house, and those benefits are obvious from the trade figures. But while our trade agreement of 1936 with the United States was followed at first by a substantial increase in trade with that country there was later a substantial decrease, and I want to assure the house from my study of our trade agreements with the United States that this will always be our experience. Our only safe and sure market is the market in Great Britain, the market of the empire, and the least sure market in which we deal at any time is the United States market; for surely that republic will take advantage of every opportunity to encourage trade on behalf of its own people, and we in Canada will suffer in consequence. I feel that this government has sold its birthright, the golden opportunity on which we were launched in 1932, and sold it for something that may look all right on the surface; but when the surface is scratched and we begin to experience the results of the agreement, after it has come into operation, we find that it is impossible for Canada to trade on an equitable basis with the great republic to the south.
In passing I want to lodge my protest against the manner in which this trade agreement was drawn up on behalf of Canada. In the United States they have a regulation that if any tariff items are to be changed or amended by a trade treaty, the industries affected must be advised and given an opportunity to present a brief or to make representations before final action is taken. But a similar situation does not prevail in this country. Our business men and industrialists are kept decidedly in the dark as to what is going on. The only thing they know about the treaty is after it has been signed and is beginning to affect their business, without their having had an opportunity to present their views or to register a protest against the provisions of the treaty. I shall not take further time on the trade treaty because we 71492-205
shall have an opportunity to discuss it at a later date. I hope that every member of this house will take an intelligent, Canadawide point of view in discussing such an important piece of legislation.
Not only do I take this government to task for the condition in which Canada finds herself economically to-day, but I would suggest that the present administration has made absolutely no headway in reducing the expenditures of government. For example, ordinary expenditures in 1936 amounted to $372,000,000, whereas in 1938 they amounted to $414,000,000, and this increase took place despite a saving of several million dollars by a process of refunding. That does not show any economy in expenditure so far as this government is concerned. This government seems to be beset with the idea of raising revenues, collecting the money and increasing the expenditures of government, rather than decreasing the costs of government and leaving in the hands of the taxpayers some money by means of which business can carry on and prosper, and unemployment be made to shrink. I think of that item of ordinary expenditures increasing, and I think of the possibilities of extravagant expenditures being found in the estimates for the coming year. I think of many of what we call in ward politics, " pork-barrel " items, that might appear in the estimates this year, to increase still further this $414,000,000 of ordinary expenditures. I think, too, of the railway deficit of over 150,000,000, and of the outlay of over $60,000,000 incurred through fixing the price for wheat. There are other items to which I could make reference; but surely, Mr. Speaker, in view of the items I have cited and the conditions that prevail in this country, this government, despite the fact that this is most likely an election year, will devise ways and means of presenting to the house estimates that will show a decided shrinkage in the cost of government so far as the dominion is concerned. If this government would set an example in economy, I believe the provincial governments would follow suit, and I believe the municipal governments would follow the lead of the provincial governments. The result would be that we would have decreased costs of all our government services, and the Canadian people would have to pay less in taxation to their various governments.
There is one item to which I wish to make special reference to-night. I am sorry the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) is not in his seat. An item has appeared in the press indicating that the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways has authorized an expenditure of $12,600,000 for work on the terminal or tunnel station at Montreal. To
The Address-Mr. Walsh

my mind this looks very much as though the Canadian National Railways was getting back into politics. We are in an election year, and here is the government getting the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways to make this expenditure of $12,600,000, spread over a period of four years.
