speechtext:
I am making the suggestion that the Canadian National Railways is getting back into politics, and it is being forced into that position by this present government. The Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) during the St. Henry by-election made use of these words:
The government of which I am a part will settle this problem of the Canadian National railway and the level crossings; we will fill the hole on Dorchester street and solve the problem of the approaches thereto.
In that he was supported by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin). I have heard in this house so frequently from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) that the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways have been completely divorced from politics; that they are not under the control of the Minister of Transport; that they are not under the control of the government, but that they are an independent body conducting the affairs of that railroad as they would conduct a corporation of their own. Yet we have during the course of a byelection statements of this kind from responsible ministers of the crown in order, with the people's own money, to purchase their support during the course of the election. Now the money is being spent: $12,600,000 of it is being spent, and for no other purpose than to purchase the votes of the electors in and around Montreal, so that this government, which is discredited in other ways, can come back into office, purchasing their way into office on the strength of bringing the Canadian National Railways back actively into politics-which we tried to avoid in 1933.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And filling holes left by the Tories.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They did not make the hole.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I ask the question seriously, and I ask the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville to give it serious consideration:

Has the Canadian National Railways got back into politics? Have we gone back to the conditions which prevailed prior to 1932? My answer is yes, and I support that answer by the suggestion that the very first act of this government was to change from a board of trustees to a board of directors. The warnings of the Duff commission were not in any way heeded by the present government. I read, on page 13 of the report of the royal commission to inquire into railways and transportation in Canada, words like these:
Running through its administrative practices, however, has been the red thread of extravagance. The disciplinary check upon undue expenditure, inherent in private corporations because of their limited financial resources, has not been in evidence. Requisitions of the management have been endorsed by governments, and successive parliaments have voted money freely, if not lavishly.
Within the railway organization there has been freedom in expenditure and encouragement in plans for expansion and extension of services which were inconsistent with prudent administrative practice. The administration failed to realize that this country, with the greatest railway mileage in the world in relation to population, could not afford further capital and maintenance expenditures for unwarranted branch lines, for de luxe services, for unrequired hotels, for the building of ships in competitive service to be shortly abandoned; and, generally, for costly adventures in competitive railways out of proportion to the needs of the.country.
I would ask hon. members, Is it the intention of the government to go back on the recommendations of this report, or are they shoving the Canadian National Railways back again into politics? I warn the government that if they do so they will get exactly the results which were experienced in this country from 1920 to 1932, the experience that is warned against in this report, and this country will be brought into a financial condition where our bonds and other securities will not be of the value they were when this government came into office in 1935.
I want to ask the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville if he recalls an item in the Duff report bearing on cooperation. If there is one place in the worid where these two railways can cooperate, it is in terminal facilities. Everyone, even the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville, knows that terminal facilities are not a paying proposition. Terminals are an expense, and if there is one place where railways can cooperate and where they do cooperate, it is in the matter of railway terminal facilities.

But I do not want hon. members to make speeches at the expense of the few minutes I have left. I want to read from page 65 of the Duff report:
We have emphasized the fact that a principal weakness of the past decade has been the failure of the railways to act together in their own interests and in the interests of the public. It is not enough that each should take all practicable measures of economy in respect of its own system. There must be joint action with a view to savings in the wider sphere.
I could go on to the next paragraph of that report, but time is short. I just wanted to use that to show hon. members that the Duff commission, after a careful study', presented a report urging cooperation, and that we in parliament at a later date, in 1933, in the Statutes of Canada 1932-33, chapter 33, sections 16 and 17, incorporated that principle, urging cooperation. I say again, and it cannot be repeated too often, that if there is one place in the whole system of these railways where cooperation could be effective without detriment to either railway and without any detriment to the people of this country, it is in railway terminals and terminal facilities. Yet this government are condoning the action of the directors of the Canadian National Railways in going ahead with this expenditure of $12,600,000. I ask this government, where does cooperation fit in with their railway policy? Have they any railway policy which is going to assist this country in curbing its $50,000,000 deficit? Do hon. members ever stop to appreciate the significance of that deficit? Practically one million dollars of our taxes is going every week to provide for the deficits of the Canadian National Railways. Yes despite that condition they are burdening the railway further with this terminal site expenditure of $12,600,000.
And that is not all, Mr. Speaker. I turn to the Palmer report. On page 9 you will find these figures, figures which show an estimated cost of $46,000,000. They have already spent S18,000,000; the balance left to complete the work is $28,000,000. The proposal is to spend
$12,600,000 during the next four years. This leaves another $15,400,000 to be spent at a later date, most likely just before another election, if this government is able to buy its way back into power at the close of the present session of parliament.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Money cannot save them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Bear in mind that these are only estimated figures; they are not final; if we have anything to go by in past estimates, government figures for government projected expenditures are very far beside the mark, and this balance of $15,000,000 which is left to be spent will doubtless be expanded to thirty or forty million dollars before that tunnel station is complete.
We have as an example of government estimating, the building of a harbour bridge in Montreal, where the estimate was $9,000,000 the final figure was $18,000,000. No doubt the tunnel station will fall into the same category. Why should there not be a union station in the city of Montreal? There are union stations at Halifax, Saint John, Quebec, Ottawa, Toronto, and other cities throughout Canada. That plan has been adopted in most of the large cities in the United States in order to save expense to the railways, and it has also been adopted in European countries. Why can we not adopt it in Canada? It would not be detrimental to either railway to have a union station in Montreal.
Again, would it not be' wise definitely to settle the railway and transportation problem in Canada before launching upon such an extravagant expenditure for something that will possibly block the future as far as Montreal is concerned and prevent our ever having union station facilities for the railways and the public travelling in and out of Montreal?
I was going to suggest that if the government is doing this work as a relief measure there are many other relief measures that could be adopted in Montreal. There are many others that would bring greater glory to the city of Montreal than the filling of that hole by a tunnel station. The tunnel station work already done there could be used to advantage for the building of a civic centre, a road approach from Victoria bridge into that hole in the ground. It could be used as an entrance and exit for buses and a tram service to parts of Montreal, and the $18,000,000 would not be at all lost. I repeat, the work already done could be used to advantage. If it is really a relief measure, then I think of those huge buildings I have spoken of on another occasion, referred to as the university of Montreal. That project is unfinished, unused. An opportunity exists
The Address-Mr. Walsh

there for a government to do a really useful piece of work for the general uplift of the whole community, because from that expenditure untold benefits could be derived through the establishment, in the way of a return on the money that might be spent, of scholarships that would enable our j'oung men to attend that university from every point in Canada. Also young French-Canadians who cannot afford it at the present time could take advantage of further education in that institution. Money spent in that way would not be ill-spent.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It was flatly refused by the previous administration.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am afraid that this government is so intent on politics that it forgets the ultimate good of Canada. Politics seems to be an obsession with this government. Why, they cannot even appoint returning officers without having politics as the predominant factor in their consideration. I had spoken to the Secretary of State about a returning officer in my division, a returning officer who was there in 1926. He was reappointed by the government in 1930 and in 1935. I had half a promise that he would be left there because he was a competent man, but he has been removed and in his place what name do I find? I find the name of the chief organizer of my Liberal opponent. He has been appointed returning officer for the constituency of Mount Royal, a position which is supposed to be held by an unbiassed public servant. I am given to understand that mine is only one example; very many others could be quoted along the same line.
There is only one other phase of government I should like to touch on in conclusion, and that is the condition we find in Canada on account of lack of cooperation on the part of this government. A complete lack of unity exists and is all too apparent. While visiting in Charlottetown I read on a tablet erected in confederation room these words:
In the hearts and the minds of the delegates who assembled in this room on September 1, 1864, was born the Dominion of Canada. Providence being their guide, they builded better than they knew.
It has been left to a Liberal government practically to undo what the fathers of confederation have done. Just take a glance over the political map of Canada and you will readily see to what I have reference. This government is not on speaking terms with the government of Alberta-not through any fault of the Alberta government. Because they were not a government after the complexion of this administration, this administration refused to consider with the Alberta

government the question of taking care of a loan that became due. It had, in my opinion, a political motive in view. That should never have been. No dominion government should allow any provincial government to fall down on the repayment of any loan secured from the public. This government says it was impossible to deal with the premier and the provincial treasurer of Alberta. I say that it was not only possible, but that it was the duty of this government to do so. It was the duty of this government to bring the premier and the treasurer of Alberta to Ottawa and to lock themselves in a room with those gentlemen and say, "We will go out of this room when this question is settled satisfactorily both to you and to ourselves." The province of Alberta had as much right to fair treatment from this government as any other provincial government in Canada. That was the beginning of a very sharp antagonism between the province of Alberta and the dominion government at present holding office.
Then we come to the older provinces of Ontario and Quebec. With regard to the present discord let me read a statement made by one of the ministers in the course of a speech. In supporting the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) said:
I subscribe most heartily to everything which Mr. Rogers has stated with regard to the alliance which exists between Premiers Hepburn and Duplessis and also with regard to the altogether deplorable effort which has been made to bring about the retirement of Premier Mackenzie King as leader of the Liberal party -a move very clearly intended to establish a government at Ottawa which would be subject to the joint control of provincial administrations in Toronto and Quebec and which as such would constitute the very antithesis of responsible government under the accepted federal system. Subterfuge must be uncovered, selfishness must be blasted asunder. We must make our stand on the solid foundation of national unity.
Do words of that sort bring about national unity? I say that such words, the irresponsible utterances of responsible ministers, create a condition which it is impossible for this government to remedy. Unity in the Dominion of Canada will never again be a recognized fact as long as the present government holds office.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is only another year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

I could go further in reading this, but the time is short. I was surprised at the bizarre utterances of these two ministers. It was a terrifying story that they had to tell at Port Arthur. These details of a conspiracy that they were going to unfold to a waiting public have not yet been told.

The Address-Mr. Brunelle
If we read such a story from Germany or Italy we would think something sinister was taking place. These responsible ministers speak of a conspiracy in this country; do they understand the terms they are using? Do they understand that national unity can never be brought about in this country by responsible ministers of the crown making such bizarre utterances? I verily thought that the days of Guy Fawkes had returned and that we had better place additional guards in the corridors and cellars of these parliament buildings to protect ourselves and even the members of this government from what might happen in the course of this conspiracy as it was being hatched. Both of these ministers have already spoken in this debate; yet we have had no unfolding of the details of this conspiracy. It is rather a bold charge. Subterfuge must be uncovered, they say; selfishness must be blasted asunder, intrigue and conspiracy must cease to flourish; yet they have given us no details. I think hon. members should demand an explanation. Men occupying high public office have had their names connected with such sinister expressions; yet we have had no explanation either in this house or in public. They go further, suggesting that the premier of Ontario and the premier of Quebec might even be conspiring with the leader of this party to get rid of this government. That is going rather too far. The object is a worthy one, but I am sure that these two premiers are not at the present time in any conspiracy -with the leader of the Conservative party here to overthrow the present government by the means suggested by the two ministers. Certainly the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) is anxious to overthrow the present government, by constitutional means-

opposition cannot be drawn into a conspiracv to get rid of the present government. To get rid of it is his duty; he is paid to do that work, but he is going to do it by educating and enlightening the public, not by associating himself with people who enter into conspiracies. It reminds me very much of Lie condition we had in Quebec prior to 1936, when the Taschereau government had outlived its usefulness. During the last two or three years of their existence, whenever any criticism was directed against them they haughtily suggested that the province of Quebec was being assailed. There was some indication of that attitude in the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King); he took us to task for not going from one end of Canada to the other to tell what this government had done for the people of Canada, which he said it was our duty to do. Although we criticize the government we are no less loyal to Canada than is the Prime Minister. We shall continue to criticize, believing that we are acting in the best interests of the people of Canada; we are trying to stir up this government to solve at least some of the major problems with which Canada is confronted.
In conclusion I agree with the statement of the premier of Ontario when he said:
I am very optimistic with regard to Ontario, but' I am most pessimistic over the condition in which we find the affairs of the dominion.
And further:
I would suggest that Mr. King lift the blinds of his summer retreat at Kingsmere, peek out, and then go back and hibernate again. It strikes me that's about all he has been doing the last four years, and he might as well continue.
On this side of the house we are in hearty agreement with those sentiments, although we cannot always agree with the person who gave utterance to them.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the several hon. members who have so justly praised the mover (Mr. Matthews) and seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Also I congratulate the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. McLarty) and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. MacKinnon) for their recent appointment as ministers of the crown. It is also a pleasant duty to felicitate the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) upon the honour which was conferred on him when he was chosen as leader of the Conservative party and leader of the opposition. I wish him courage and patience.
Before I came to Ottawa for this session I heard a great many contradictory comments about the leader of the opposition. I even heard it said that he is a self-made man. Of course I reserved my judgment. But when I listened to his speech last week and saw the rather rude way in which he was treating the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who is usually so kind and considerate of his political opponents, I did form my opinion; I came to the conclusion that the leader of the opposition is a self-made man, and thus Providence
The Address-Mr. Brunelle

escaped a great responsibility. Many hon. members of this chamber knew him and sat with him in this house in previous sessions. It was therefore particularly interesting for a new member like myself to listen to the three-hour speech that he made at the beginning of last week. I dare say new members could not help thinking that he is capable of saying a great many things. I expected in the first place that he would refer to the different reforms which he wishes to bring about in this country. I expected also that, he would make a new declaration as to immigration, those fifty or seventy-five million people whom he wishes to bring to this country, as stated by himself at the meeting which he held in Toronto in July shortly after he was chosen as leader of the Conservative party. Let me read the report which I saw in Le Devoir of July 22, shortly after that meeting:
R. J. Manion in favour of immigration. There is room in this country, he said, for 50 to 75 million people. If we adopt a -wise immigration policy, there is no limit to the future development of the Canadian nation.
That statement, of course, was quite consistent with the program-

Dr. Manion, the leader of the Conservative party, declared last night his categorical opposition to the admission of immigrants to this country when there are so many unemployed Canadians.

The fact is that the Conservative party is pledged to a policy of immigration. Allow me to read from the platform of the Conservative party, adopted at the convention held last July in the city of Toronto:
In order to ensure a continuance of the British connection and Canadian participation in the benefits that accrue from membership in the British commonwealth of nations and the economic welfare and safety of Canada, this party recognizes the immediate necessity of our government's approaching the government of the United Kingdom and discussing and deciding upon a policy for the selected migration of British families from Great Britain and Ireland under a carefully prepared plan whereby ample and proper provision will be made for British finance and supervision and the return of families found unable to fit into the national and economic life of Canada; and be it further understood that similar advantages be extended to France.
To confirm this view the right hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Bennett), at a banquet tendered to him in the city of Toronto on the 16th of this month, declared:
It is urgent that Canada's gates be opened to immigrants. . . . Canada should welcome newcomers to help develop the raw materials possessed here in such abundance.
The leader of the Conservative party in the senate also was present and apparently gave his blessing to that statement. When the platform of the Conservative party is in favour of a policy of immigration; when all

I quote:
It is permissible to suggest that the conclave of federal Toryism just ended heralds the decline of a once great party to the status now occupied by Liberalism in Great Britain. This view is based less upon the selection of Dr. Manion as a leader, than it is upon the almost incredibly weak and innocuous program which the master minds of the party drafted as a platform. The chief defect of the new platform is its failure to express any definite political philosophy .	.	. the strategy of
course, is to avoid having a definite platform which will invite attack, and to win on the mistakes that the Liberal government may be expected to make. In other words, the game which the Conservative convention played politically was the old game of "Ins" vs. "Outs."
Speaking for my constituents, [DOT] sir, I say I am opposed to immigration. Let our abundant raw materials be developed and exploited by our own Canadians who are now without work. I congratulate the government upon not allowing the entry of immigrants into Canada. I congratulate the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) upon the statement he made recently in the city of Montreal, to the effect that the government was not in favour
of amending the restrictions in regard to immigration. I want to be placed on record as one who objects strongly to the entry of Jews, en masse or otherwise, into our country. I hasten to say that I have no brief against the Hebrew race; but since through all the ages they have been the cause, justly or unjustly, of great difficulties in various countries, I say we must take care. History repeats itself. I have deep sympathy for the Jews who are now being persecuted in certain countries of Europe; I think their situation is deplorable; but at the present time in our own country we have thousands of fellow citizens whose situation is also deplorable, and I believe that charity begins at home. I do not want one job in Canada to be taken by an immigrant, be he a Jew or otherwise, so long as we must spend money for relief. It is known by all hon. members that for the most part Jews inhabit only the cities and towns. If they are admitted they will either find jobs or be thrown on relief. We have at present too many people on relief, and if there are jobs available they should be given to our fellow citizens. I dislike reading press reports to the effect that the government in London or some English societies wish to assist the Jews by sending them to the colonies-and in that statement they include Canada. May I point out that we are not a colony. To preach charity and generosity, and then to practise those virtues at the expense of someone else is not a worthy procedure.
I now approach a more pleasant subject. May I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) upon the treaty with the United States he signed in 1935, and upon the one signed more recently. A greater trade within Canada and a greater exchange of goods with other nations will help to solve unemployment. At the risk of repeating what other members have said. I would point out that the exchange of goods between nations will help primary and secondary producers and will give more employment to a greater number of people. New industries will establish themselves in Canada, as it becomes known that their products can be exported to other countries. It is in great part on account of the fiscal and commercial policy of this government that a new industry called International Foils has erected a large plant in my native city of Cap de la Madeleine. The entire production of the plant is to be exported. Could that industry have established itself in Canada if there had been no exportation facilities or the possibility of exchanging its products for other articles which Canadians require?
The problem of unemployment will be at least partly solved if we have a sufficient
30G
The Address-Mr. Brunette

number of new industries in Canada. Another partial solution lies in the exploitation of our natural resources, the greatest of which is agriculture. There is plenty of unbroken land awaiting cultivation and occupation. Let the provincial governments, which control colonization, undertake a serious back-to-the-land movement. Let them pay the unemployed to improve our unbroken lands and thereby make them attractive, remunerative and suitable for settlers. Large areas of partly improved land are to be found in several of the older and more settled districts. Those lands are lying idle and unproductive, despite the fact that there are highways, railways, schools and churches to be used by settlers who would need only a little assistance for purposes of exploitation. I feel so certain that a real back-to-the-land movement is urgent that I never miss an opportunity to speak about it.
The fact that I prepared this speech on the train may have directed my thoughts to the situation as regards railway station accommodation in the city of Montreal. I have thought, too, of the large sums of money the railways have cost Canada. My mind goes back to the millions of dollars which are about to be spent on the erection of a Canadian National Railway terminus in Montreal. If we must do work to relieve unemployment-and I think we must-it is urgent to choose the most useful way of spending public funds. Until the contrary has been shown to me, I shall hold that we should make a union station out of the present Windsor station to serve the western part of Montreal, another union station out of the present Viger station to serve the east end of the city, and eliminate that miserable and pitiful stopping place now known as Moreau station. I shall say no more on the subject and shall be content to await the views of my colleagues representing the city of Montreal.
